title: KVCache Cache in the Wild — production KV reuse characterization

fields.detail: Published 2025-06-03, cs.DC. Canonical production measurement that bounds how much multi-turn reuse there really is. Abstract: "KV$ reuses are skewed across requests, where reuses between single-turn requests are equally important as multi-turn requests; the reuse time and probability are diverse considering all requests, but for a specific request category, the pattern tends to be predictable; and the overall cache size required for an ideal cache hit ratio is moderate." The HTML gives the more actionable finding for a single GPU: "The lifespan of KV$ is ephemeral: the P99 lifespan of KV$ in to-B workloads is 97 seconds, so a small cache is typically sufficient for the KV$ cache." Trace source: "we collected and characterized two representative production serving workloads from one of the world's largest cloud providers (Aliyun)".

title: Zipage — compressed paged attention that supports prefix caching

fields.detail: Published 2026-03-01, cs.DC. Answers "can token eviction for reasoning coexist with paged/prefix-cached serving". "This paper introduces Compressed PagedAttention, a method that combines token-wise KV cache eviction with PagedAttention. We propose a comprehensive scheduling strategy and support prefix caching and asynchronous compression for Compressed PagedAttention. Based on this, we have developed a high-concurrency LLM inference engine, Zipage. On large-scale mathematical reasoning tasks, Zipage achieves around 95% of the performance of Full KV inference engines while delivering over 2.1x speedup."

title: SONIC — segment-level compression of dialogue history

fields.detail: Published 2026-01-29, cs.CL. Answers multi-turn history compression with learned rather than heuristic eviction. "The linear growth of Key-Value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for multi-turn LLM deployment. Existing KV cache compression methods often fail to account for the structural properties of multi-turn dialogues, relying on heuristic eviction that risks losing critical context. We propose SONIC, a learning-based framework that compresses historical segments into compact and semantically rich Nexus tokens." Reported result: "at compression ratios of 80% and 50%, SONIC consistently outperforms baselines such as H2O and StreamingLLM on four diverse multi-turn benchmarks." ---

title: Should the scheduler order the waiting queue by cache affinity (the ordering half of prefix-cache payoff)?

fields.who is still asking: fululi12 / vLLM project — open PR #54625 "[Core][V1] Add cache-aware admission ordering"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Within a bounded look-ahead window over the waiting queue, admit requests whose prefix is already resident in the KV cache ahead of requests that would have to compute theirs. The problem is an interaction between strict FCFS admission and prefix caching: a cold request admitted first allocates blocks, and under pressure that allocation evicts blocks which a request further back in the queue still needs. The eviction turns a would-be cache hit into recomputation, and the deeper the shared prefix, the more expensive the loss."
fields.what specifically is missing: The feature is not merged and both flags are off by default — "Two new scheduler options, both off by default: --cache-aware-admission-window N, default 0 ... --cache-aware-admission-threshold F, default 0.0". Scope is also explicitly restricted: "It requires the fcfs policy. Positional reordering is meaningless in a priority heap".

title: How is a practitioner supposed to measure prefix cache effectiveness at all?

fields.who is still asking: SarnadAbhilash / vLLM project — open PR #53395 "[Docs] Explain how to measure prefix cache effectiveness"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "The Automatic Prefix Caching guide explains where APC helps, but does not currently tell operators how to measure cache effectiveness or distinguish token reuse from end-to-end performance gains. This change: documents the token units of vllm:prefix_cache_queries and vllm:prefix_cache_hits ; adds a PromQL example for aggregate token hit ratio; describes how to control request order, concurrency, and initial cache state for comparisons; recommends reporting TTFT, latency, and throughput alongside hit ratio; clarifies that decode, scheduling, eviction, routing, and block alignment can make a high hit ratio differ from the observed speedup"
fields.what specifically is missing: A shipped, documented procedure for measuring prefix-cache benefit and for separating token reuse from end-to-end gain. This PR is still open (opened 2026-08-22) and is docs-only. **The PR body also contains the single most direct measured answer found anywhere to "does prefix caching pay off for agentic traffic":** "This guidance is informed by an isolated prefix-cache experiment in which a 94.59% full-block token hit ratio produced only a 5.7%–6.2% throughput improvement for a short agentic workload at concurrency 64." Related and closed-as-not-planned: issue #54607 at https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54607 — "[Doc]: --prefix-match-unit and the default match granularity are undocumented" (stateReason NOT_PLANNED; the page shows the stale label and no human resolution comment was retrievable), whose body records the practical cost of the gap: "Spent longer than I'd like to admit chasing a 0% prefix cache hit rate that turned out to be correct... title: How should hybrid Mamba/GDN cached state be thinned under LRU pressure?

fields.who is still asking: alphabetc1 / SGLang — Draft PR #38000 "[Mamba] Thin cached states by coverage instead of evicting the LRU tail"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "[Mamba] Thin cached states by coverage instead of evicting the LRU tail"
fields.what specifically is missing: The PR motivation gives the precise failure mode for a **branching shared prefix on a single GPU**: "On a hybrid Mamba/GDN model every chunked-prefill boundary donates one Mamba state into the radix tree, so a long prompt pushes len / chunked_prefill_size states through the Mamba LRU. The LRU evicts a path's states shallow-first (they were inserted first), which is the inverse of what a branch match needs: a request that shares a 40k prefix and diverges mid-way is gated on the Mamba state at the divergence point, and the shallow states are exactly the ones that are gone. With the KV fully resident, cached_tokens drops to 0 with no error. Reproduced on upstream main (Qwen3.5-4B, 1xH200, extra_buffer, 3.3M-token KV pool so KV is never the constraint), 3 distinct 32k chains then fork chain 0 at 8192 and re-send every chain, --max-mamba-cache-size 48 --max-running-requests 4 --chunked-prefill-size 2048". It is filed as a Draft and references "#36935 (and the LRU-pressure half of #30314's discussion)". Related open correctness work: SGLang Draft PR #39263 "Fix hybrid session references after an empty terminal cache insert", which is explicitly "Follow-up correctness fix for the session-reference support in #29173, not a new retention policy."

title: Nobody measures repeated compaction over the horizon an agent actually runs

fields.who is still asking: the authors of "What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate-Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents" (arXiv 2607.08032)

title: Prefix caching for small reasoning models — measured to make serving WORSE

fields.who: Qi Li et al. (HKUST-GZ), paper "Reasoning Language Model Inference Serving Unveiled: An Empirical Study"
fields.closure status: Not a PR — this is a PUBLISHED paper whose own experiments conclude the technique does not pay off in the relevant regime. This is the single most consequential negative finding for the target researcher (Qwen3-4B is the 4B scale).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "However, for 7B models, prefix caching negatively impacts efficiency, leading to increased latency."
fields.additional retrieved detail: The paper has a dedicated subsection "5.3 Is Prefix Caching Useful for Contributing Efficient RLLM Serving?" and its abstract states the general finding: "model quantization methods and speculative decoding can improve service system efficiency with small compromise to RLLM accuracy, while prefix caching, KV cache quantization may even degrade accuracy or serving performance for small RLLM." The contrast is explicit: "We find that for sufficiently large RLLMs (14B and above), prefix caching significantly improves runtime speed and serving metrics without compromising performance." The breakdown is in Appendix J.3 ("Prefix Caching Full results") with paired tables (e.g. "Table 14: Results of RLLM-7B without Prefix Cache"). Environment: "All of our experiments are running on three devices: a server with 8 RTX A6000 GPUs with 48GB VRAM, a server equipped with 8 RTX 4090 GPUs with 24GB VRAM, and a server with 8 NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB GPUs" with "vLLM version 0.8.1 and SGLang version 0.4.6.post1". The paper's own limitations undercut generality: "our hardware resources were limited, and we aim to extend our evaluations to a wider range of hardware platforms in the future."

title: Elastic KV Cache — reclaiming the prefill-activation reserve

fields.closure status: Published paper reporting an explicit negative result on its own premise (and a note that prefix caching still works with the mechanism).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Having built the mechanism, we test the premise it rests on and report an honest negative result. It only pays off if a small prefill chunk size badly hurts prefill latency. In a controlled experiment injecting long prompts into a live decode load, that penalty is small (median time-to-first-token differs by about 1% between chunk sizes of 8192 and 32768 tokens), because prefill is compute bound and decode consumes only about one token per sequence per step. Simply lowering max_num_batched_tokens recovers more KV than the controller does, at nearly equal latency."
fields.additional retrieved detail: Relevant to a single-GPU deployment because the win dilutes with parallelism: "The reserve also dilutes under tensor parallelism, from 16% of KV at TP1 to 2.7% at TP4." Testbed (so this one is NOT hardware-ruled-out for the researcher): "All measurements are on a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in float16, vLLM 0.23.0, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9 and max_model_len=32768 unless stated otherwise." It also confirms compatibility with the reuse path: the mechanism "works with CUDA graphs and prefix caching".

title: Immediate online KV compaction for agents

fields.who: authors of "Practical Online KV Cache Compaction for LLM Agents: An Empirical Study"
fields.closure status: Published empirical study whose headline result is that the naive (immediate) form of the technique hurts. The negative finding is the paper's main contribution.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus and WideSearch show that immediate compaction often hurts performance, whereas delaying compaction to use the agent's future queries recovers much of the gap. Moreover, TE is often more robust than AM under imperfect proxies."
fields.additional retrieved detail: The structural reason is stated in the abstract: "most prior methods assume a static context where future queries are known or can be approximated offline. Agents instead require online compaction: new information must be compressed before future relevance is known, using proxy queries cheap enough for the inference path." Best reported positive: "Across models at different scales, TE preserves most of the accuracy while reducing KV cache by 80%, and can improve throughput over the no compaction baseline."

title: vLLM — Hybrid checkpoint ABI for non-KV prefix resume (RFC)

fields.closure status: Closed as NOT_PLANNED with the `stale` label. CLOSURE WAS BY AUTOMATED STALE BOT; no human maintainer reason is present on the page.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "This issue has been automatically closed due to inactivity. Please feel free to reopen if you feel it is still relevant. Thank you!"
fields.additional retrieved detail: This is the open/shut case for "what breaks cross-turn reuse when the engine's reused state is not pure KV". "Prefix caching is comparatively clean for transformer KV state because the cache object and the reuse boundary align closely. Hybrid models complicate that with non-KV state such as recurrent state, conv buffers, and local-window or hybrid side state. That state is often updated in place, materialized differently across phases, backend-specific in storage layout, and not safely validated by raw backing-buffer equality alone." The RFC also documents a real agentic tool-calling corruption from it: "Before the fix, repeated replay was fast but wrong: cache hits were real and TTFT collapsed, but a request that previously emitted a web_search tool call would instead terminate with stop and no tool call on replay." And it confirms the gap is still documented as open upstream: "Public vLLM docs already describe hybrid cache coordination and still note that Mamba-style prefix caching is a work in progress."

title: Nexus — the off-anchor KV splice boundary, and a drift gate that does not predict drift

fields.who: Mustafa Arslan, "Nexus: Depth-Adaptive KV-Cache Splicing and Retrieval-Decoupled Tool Routing for Agentic LLMs on Unified Memory"
fields.closure status: Published paper containing two explicit self-declared negative results that bound the technique. The KV-splice lever — the part relevant to shared-prefix/content-addressed reuse of tool schemas — is the part that is bounded.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Two negative results bound the design: the off-anchor RoPE fidelity boundary, and the failure of a reference-free drift gate to predict drift (Spearman rho = 0.193)."
fields.additional retrieved detail: The mechanism's limits are stated concretely: "As a secondary, bounded lever we transplant a compiled schema KV block directly into the live context. This is fundamentally limited by rotary position embedding (RoPE) phase drift: an anchored splice is output-exact, but off-anchor placement corrupts attention, so beyond a threshold P=256 Nexus repairs the seam with a depth-adaptive suffix redecode that escalates to a full re-prefill. The resulting never-regress property is a guarantee on output fidelity (top-1 agreement, D_KL approx. 0) — not on latency, which can dip to 0.98x before converging to parity". Scope caveat: "All benchmarks were executed on an Apple M4 Max SoC (16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, 16-core Neural Engine) equipped with 64 GB Unified Memory and a 1 TB NVMe SSD" — the quantitative envelope is platform-specific.

title: Cartridges are monolithic and non-compositional — naive mixing collapses to chance

fields.who: Momchil Hardalov, Gonzalo Iglesias, Adrià de Gispert, "Cartridges at Scale: Training Modular KV Caches over Large Document Collections"
fields.closure status: Published paper whose premise check is a negative result on the naive form of trainable shared-prefix KV caches (the "cartridge" line of work).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "A critical limitation of this approach is that cartridges are monolithic and non-compositional: encoding an entire collection into a single KV block does not scale, and naively mixing cartridges trained in isolation collapses performance to near chance."
fields.additional retrieved detail: The repair is itself training-based and needs a GPU↔storage rotation: "a training framework for scalable multi-cartridge learning with dynamic distractor mixing and a memory-efficient budget manager that rotates hundreds of per-document cartridges between GPU and persistent storage." It also documents the residual gap even after the fix: "Oracle cartridge accuracy falls within 2-6 points of full in-context learning even at high compression."

title: External (CPU/NVMe) KV caching falls below break-even on a large GPU

fields.who: py-kvcache authors (AtLarge group, VU Amsterdam), "Building py-kvcache: A Performance Characterization of External KV Caching for vLLM with NVMe SSDs"
fields.closure status: Published characterization whose conclusion is that the external-tier technique does not pay off in the large-GPU / short-prefix regime — a direct caution for a 96GB single-GPU deployment.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Bailian trace replays improve TTFT on a weaker GPU, but on an H100 the average request falls below the break-even point and GPU memory alone retains enough prefixes. External KV caching should therefore be treated as a setup specific admission decision."
fields.additional retrieved detail: "Their average request length is below the measured 6,203 token SSD break-even point for Qwen3 4B, on our setup, and the H100's larger GPU memory retains a large portion of the working set. As a result the TTFT of only using GPU prefix caching is identical to that of py-kvcache". The paper also frames the general trap: "External caching is not automatically beneficial, since a cache hit replaces GPU prefill computation with cache lookup, disk or host memory reads, and ..." It does report multi-turn positives on the smaller tier: "LongBench and SCBench show that these benefits extend to irregular prefix chains and multi-turn workloads."

title: CacheScout — agent-aware KV-cache runtime for multi-agent serving

fields.hardware requirement: 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 96 GB each (plus a 4× H200 TP run for the large-model study)
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Testbed. We run experiments on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, each with 96 GB of memory. We use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the main model and run all systems under the same vLLM configuration, GPU memory budget, decoding parameters, and prefix cache settings." The large-model arm is separately multi-GPU: "CacheScout on Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 (tensor parallelism over four H200 GPUs)."
fields.why it matters for this subsection: This is the closest published system to the researcher's exact question (agentic multi-turn KV reuse, tool-call stalls, shared agent anchors, prefix caching), and it is exactly the class that is NOT reproducible on one GPU. Its diagnosis of the default engine behaviour is nevertheless directly quotable: "Existing LLM serving systems, however, manage KV-cache reactively using prefix caching and recency-based replacement, causing reusable agent contexts to be evicted before their next invocation and forcing repeated recomputation" and "Agentic workloads interleave LLM generation with external function calls; while a tool runs, the GPU pauses, the session's KV is evicted under concurrent traffic, and the next step pays a costly re-prefill when the tool returns." Implementation is "a lightweight runtime layer on top of vLLM v0.11 (V1 engine), consisting of approximately 2,300 lines of runtime logic and an 800-line patch" modifying "five vLLM source files (the block pool, the engine core, the scheduler, and the scheduler- and worker-side halves of the CPU-offload connector)".

title: Multi-turn LLM conversations under LRU — hit-ratio theory validated on P/D-disaggregated NPUs

fields.hardware requirement: 5× Ascend 910B2 NPUs with prefill/decode disaggregation (1 prefiller + 4 decoders)
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Our experiments run Qwen3-8B on five Ascend 910B2 NPUs using a Prefill-Decode disaggregation architecture, with one NPU as the prefiller and four as the decoder pool. Each NPU provides approximately 64 GB of HBM, and the model is deployed under BF16 precision." (next sentence continues: "We reserve 40 GB of the prefiller HBM for the KV cache, such that the block capacity is N = 2,275")
fields.why it matters for this subsection: This is the only theoretical treatment found of the exact quantity the subsection asks about (multi-turn KV hit ratio under LRU with growing prefixes), but the validation build is a 5-device disaggregated cluster, not one GPU. Also useful as a CLOSED-adjacent datapoint: it reports that with "P99 lifespan of KV$ ... 97 seconds" style ephemerality, only a modest capacity is needed — the paper's framing is "a practical guideline for memory capacity provisioning."

title: psRL — training-time prefix sharing for agentic RL

fields.hardware requirement: multi-node GPU cluster, 4× 80GB A100 per node, 200 Gb/s intra-node and 100 Gb/s RDMA cross-node; the industrial config spans 1536 GPUs
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Hardware settings. We deploy psRL on a large-scale GPU cluster. Specifically, each node is equipped with four 80 GB NVIDIA A100 GPUs and powered by the Intel Xeon Gold 6342 CPU with 48 physical cores and 128 GB host DRAM. Within each node, GPUs are connected via a 200 Gb/s interconnect, while cross-node communication is supported by a 100 Gb/s RDMA network fabric." and "For the industrial DTN Agent based on Qwen3-235B, we adopt a larger configuration with DP=4, TP=4, Expert Parallelism (EP)=8, and PP=12, distributing the model across 1536 GPUs."
fields.why it matters for this subsection: It is the training-side analogue of shared-prefix KV dedup across agentic samples ("production traces reveal substantial prefix redundancy across training samples") and therefore out of scope for a single-GPU inference node, but its KV-manager ideas (reference-counted block retention across samples) overlap conceptually with inference-time session management.

title: vLLM prefix-cache hash algorithm selection (collision resistance)

fields.detail: The vLLM APC design doc now documents a selectable hash algorithm and states the historical collision weakness was removed. Verbatim from the retrieved page: "In previous versions, the hash key was not guaranteed to be collision-free. As of v0.11, the default hashing algorithm is `sha256`, which addresses collision risks." title: vLLM reproducibility contract and `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`

fields.detail: The vLLM Reproducibility page (page footer dated April 28, 2026) gives the shipped answer for KV-dependent reproducibility. Verbatim: "vLLM does not guarantee the reproducibility of the results by default, for the sake of performance. To achieve reproducible results: In offline mode, you can either set VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0 which makes scheduling deterministic, or enable batch invariance to make the outputs insensitive to scheduling. In online mode, you can only enable batch invariance." The batch-invariance page (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/batch_invariance/, footer dated September 7, 2026, READ BODY) documents `export VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` and its own limits verbatim: "Batch invariance is currently in beta. Some features are still under active development." and "Enabling batch invariance may impact performance compared to the default non-deterministic mode. This trade-off is intentional to guarantee reproducibility." Hardware requirement stated on the same page: "NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or higher." Tested models include "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-AWQ" and "Qwen/Qwen3-8B". Note the causal link to KV: the source tree shows cascade attention is switched off under this flag — `vllm/config/vllm.py:1795-1800`: "Disabling cascade attention when VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT is enabled."

title: vLLM prefix-cache hit-rate counters and their design rationale

fields.detail: The Metrics design doc lists verbatim: "`vllm:prefix_cache_queries` (Counter) - Number of prefix cache queries." and "`vllm:prefix_cache_hits` (Counter) - Number of prefix cache hits." Under "Prefix Cache metrics" the doc explains the measurement choice verbatim: "Every time the prefix cache is queried, we record the number of tokens queried and the number of queried tokens present in the cache (i.e. hits). However, the metric of interest is the hit rate - i.e. the number of hits per query. ... To achieve this, we should record the queries and hits as counters in Prometheus, rather than recording the hit rate as a gauge." It also documents the logging-side estimator verbatim: "The prefix cache hit rate over the most recent 1k kv-cache block queries". Confirmed in the local source: `vllm/v1/metrics/loggers.py:584-601` defines `vllm:prefix_cache_queries` / `vllm:prefix_cache_hits`.

title: vLLM KV block residency/eviction metrics

fields.detail: Section "KV Cache Residency Metrics" verbatim: "We also emit a set of histograms that describe how long sampled KV cache blocks stay resident and how often they are reused. Sampling (`--kv-cache-metrics-sample`) keeps the overhead tiny; when a block is chosen we record: lifetime – allocation ⟶ eviction; idle before eviction – last touch ⟶ eviction; reuse gaps – the pauses between touches when the block gets reused". The exposed Prometheus metric names verbatim: "`vllm:kv_block_lifetime_seconds` – how long each sampled block exists. `vllm:kv_block_idle_before_evict_seconds` – idle tail after the final access. `vllm:kv_block_reuse_gap_seconds` – time between consecutive touches." Stated use verbatim: "Looking at lifetime and idle time on one chart makes it easy to spot stranded cache or workloads that pin prompts for a long decode."

title: SGLang deterministic inference and its radix-cache compatibility matrix

fields.detail: Documents `--enable-deterministic-inference` (flag; default: disabled). The page states the root cause verbatim: "The main source is varying batch sizes. Different batch sizes cause GPU kernels to split reduction operations differently, leading to different addition orders. Due to floating-point non-associativity ((a + b) + c ≠ a + (b + c)), this produces different results even for identical inputs." It claims verbatim: "Building on Thinking Machines Lab's batch-invariant operators, SGLang achieves fully deterministic inference while maintaining compatibility with chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, radix cache, and non-greedy sampling." The feature-compatibility table for the KV-relevant axis reads verbatim: FlashInfer → Radix Cache "❌ No"; FlashAttention 3 (FA3) → Radix Cache "✅ Yes"; Triton → Radix Cache "✅ Yes". It also ships a radix-specific determinism test verbatim: "python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --test-mode radix_cache" with "Expected result: All tests should show `Unique samples: 1` (perfectly deterministic)." This documented "FA3 + radix = Yes" is directly contradicted by ABANDONED-1.

title: SGLang HiCache L1/L2/L3 including a file (disk) backend

fields.detail: Verbatim: "HiCache organizes GPU memory as L1, host memory as L2, and distributed storage as L3." and "The file backend writes to /tmp/hicache by default (SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR overrides it), which is node-local unless that path is a shared mount." A directly relevant scope limitation is stated verbatim: "L2 is node-local and instance-private. It is host memory owned by one inference instance's process, so two instances never read each other's L2, not even two instances on the same node. A KV cache produced by instance 0 becomes visible to instance 1 only after it reaches L3."

title: Prefix caching measurably changes agent trajectories (published measurement)

fields.detail: Title "Same Request, Different Answer: Quantization Amplifies Cache-Induced Divergence in LLM Serving", submitted 2026-09-04. Verbatim from the abstract: "Enabling the cache changed the agent's trajectory on 36.2 percent of episodes at 16-bit precision and on 75.0 percent at four-bit, a gradient that survives re-measurement under a controlled cache configuration. title: Eviction error certificates via randomized eviction design

fields.detail: Title "Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design", submitted 2026-07-23, rev 2026-08-29. Verbatim: "We replace the deterministic tail with Poisson sampling at known inclusion probabilities, which makes the eviction error identifiable and turns a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set into a per-step error certificate at one extra scalar per retained token." and the impossibility result verbatim: "We prove that no estimator computable from the information a deterministic scheme retains is consistent for its own eviction error: evicted values can be altered so that everything retained is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows without bound." Reported coverage verbatim: "the certificate covers the realized attention error in 96.9--97.7\% of 12{,}096 replay cells and in 98.1--99.7\% on twelve further architectures."

title: Matched-budget audit showing the compression-evaluation protocol decides the ranking

fields.detail: Title "How Query Visibility Changes KV-Cache Compression Rankings: A Matched-Budget Audit", submitted 2026-07-11. Verbatim: "KV-cache compression methods are predominantly evaluated with the query appended to the context before compression -- a query-aware protocol. Yet the economic case for a compressed KV cache is reuse: compress a document once, answer many future questions against it." and "Three findings. (1) Query visibility changes the rankings: under the agnostic protocol, of the five audited methods that share a common attention backend, only KeyDiff beats a best-of-3 trivial baseline consistently (31 of 36 cells), and the most widely deployed method, SnapKV, loses to "keep the start and the recent window" on average (-0.066)." Scale verbatim: "144,300 paired evaluations on RULER-8192; 40,800 on LongBench; 50,000-resample paired bootstrap throughout".

title: SSD-resident KV without the kernel filesystem

fields.detail: Title "Unified KV Pooling to Accelerate Long-Context LLM Serving", submitted 2026-06-10. Verbatim: "unified KV pooling, which aggregates multiple host-memory modules and SSDs into a single logical pool and distributes KV caches across devices based on their bandwidth. To eliminate the filesystem overhead, we design KV-passthrough, which bypasses the kernel filesystem and directly accesses SSD-resident KV caches from user space via SPDK." Reported result verbatim: "unified KV pooling reduces TTFT in long-contexts ~4.1x over state-of-the-art techniques, all making under 10 s. It also reduces blocked I/O time by up to 23.2x by eliminating filesystem overhead." Retrieved testbed sentence verbatim (this is a single-GPU setup, so NOT hardware-ruled-out): "We use Qwen3-30B-A3B [18] on a server equipped with an NVIDIA H100-80GB GPU, two 64 GB DDR4 host-memory modules with a combined peak bandwidth of 21.3 GB/s, and two 2 TB NVMe SSDs connected through PCIe 5.0×16 with a combined peak bandwidth of 63 GB/s." Its own limitation, verbatim: "Our current implementation relies on SPDK polling for SSD I/O completion. While polling eliminates the kernel interrupt path and reduces I/O latency, it increases CPU utilization due to continuous queue checking."

Reported result verbatim: "unified KV pooling reduces TTFT in long-contexts ~4.1x over state-of-the-art techniques, all making under 10 s. It also reduces blocked I/O time by up to 23.2x by eliminating filesystem overhead." Retrieved testbed sentence verbatim (this is a single-GPU setup, so NOT hardware-ruled-out): "We use Qwen3-30B-A3B [18] on a server equipped with an NVIDIA H100-80GB GPU, two 64 GB DDR4 host-memory modules with a combined peak bandwidth of 21.3 GB/s, and two 2 TB NVMe SSDs connected through PCIe 5.0×16 with a combined peak bandwidth of 63 GB/s." Its own limitation, verbatim: "Our current implementation relies on SPDK polling for SSD I/O completion. While polling eliminates the kernel interrupt path and reduces I/O latency, it increases CPU utilization due to continuous queue checking."

title: vLLM PoC "soft-pin recently-hit prefix-cache entries" — closed by author as a workaround

fields.closure status: PR closed unmerged by the author
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Closing this too — same reasoning as #43302 (close comment). @stecasta's block-pool instrumentation on the #42948 thread (comment) shows the real bug is 131% pool overflow from the homogeneous lcm=256 physical block layout vs DSv4-Flash's {256, 64, 4, 8}-block-size KV groups. Under that overflow, some eviction every alloc cycle is mandatory; the recent-hit set in this PR can only delay the eviction of blocks that have already served a lookup hit, which by itself doesn't help the agentic-rotation case (per @stecasta's BS-sweep: 46% at BS=4, 21% at BS=8 — meaningful mitigation but not a fix). The real avenue is heterogeneous per-page-size pools so the bs=4 SWA indexer stops costing 64× its useful storage: #42082 (RFC) + #42374 (WIP). Closing this PR rather than leaving a workaround in the review queue."
fields.date: created May 18, 2026; closed May 21, 2026. The PR's own "Known limitations" section stated verbatim: "Heuristic, not principled. "Was hit recently" is a proxy for "will likely be hit again". It works for the chat-template-prelude pattern but adds policy where the original code had clean LRU semantics. Very-high-churn workloads could outrun the recent-hit set." and "Doesn't address the architectural mismatch. vLLM conflates "free physical block" with "cached prefix entry"; a two-tier pool, refcount-based pinning, or stale-marking on eviction would all be cleaner long-term solutions."

title: vLLM multi-storage replication for shared-prefix KV blocks — closed after independent testing showed it was a regression

fields.who: manueldomke (vLLM contributor); independent test by stecasta
fields.closure status: PR closed unmerged by the author. **The failure was caught by an independent reproduction, not by the author's own benchmark.**
fields.stated reason, verbatim (author's close: "Pre-reserving 4 GB of pristine blocks (the mechanism in this PR) under that constraint makes the regression strictly worse: effective pool drops ~10%, eviction pressure rises, even the chat-template prelude survivors get wiped. Hence the 0% hit rate. The mechanism does demonstrably help the one-shared-prefix-across-many-sessions shape my reproducer tested (chat-completion with large system prompt, RAG with shared retrieval context), and the 4-step #42948 issue-body reproducer hits 99.95% on A.3 with this PR. But those are narrower than the agentic-rotation case that drives the real production pain, and shipping a connector that worsens the more-common workload to land a narrower one isn't acceptable." and "Thanks to @stecasta for the careful re-test that prevented this from being merged as a regression."
fields.date: created May 21, 2026; closed May 21, 2026. The independent test result, verbatim from stecasta in issue #42948: "| BS | N | Vanilla hit | This PR hit | This PR wall vs nocache baseline | ... | 4 | 8 | 1.0% | **0.0%** | +10% slower (348 s vs 317 s) | | 8 |16 | 0.3% | **0.0%** | +13% slower (581 s vs 514 s) |" and "Both prefix_cache_hit_rate and external_prefix_cache_hit_rate reported 0% throughout."

fields.closure status: published negative result — the paper's own result undercuts the evaluation practice it audits ("KV cache compression is commonly evaluated by final-answer accuracy").
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We test this assumption for large reasoning models and show that it can fail: under compression, correct answers and the validity of their visible supporting rationales can be preserved at different rates." and "Across tasks, token-eviction methods can preserve competitive final-answer accuracy while substantially degrading chain support or perturbation faithfulness. We call this the answer-evidence gap."

title: SSD-backed KV restore is "no longer beneficial" below a 98.3% hit rate (Tutti's own measurement)

fields.who: authors of "Tutti: Making SSD-Backed KV Cache Practical for Long-Context LLM Serving" (arXiv 2605.03375)
fields.closure status: not a closure — a published measurement inside a paper that undercuts the general technique it then improves. Recorded as ABANDONED-class per the negative-result rule.
fields.stated reason, verbatim (retrieved from: //arxiv.org/html/2605.03375v1): "restoring KV cache from SSDs is no longer beneficial (vLLM v0.12.0 vs. v0.17.0)" and "Critically, for our system, this crossover point is pushed to an extremely high cache hit rate of 98.3%, a significant improvement compared to the much lower thresholds observed in the LMCache-SSD baseline." and "Applying layer-wise transfers on SSDs (SSD-LW) further reduces I/O granularity and increases the number of operations, inflating end-to-end latency and pushing GPU bubble time to around 80% of total inference latency."

title: vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (hash-based block cache)

fields.detail: The canonical vLLM design doc for prefix KV reuse, retrieved live. It states the value proposition and the implementation choice verbatim: "Since prefix caching is almost a free lunch and won't change model outputs, it has been widely used by many public endpoints (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) and most open source LLM inference frameworks (e.g., SGLang)." And: "While there are many ways to implement prefix caching, vLLM chooses a hash-based approach." The doc specifies the key components and two hard constraints: "We only cache full blocks." And on hashing: "In previous versions, the hash key was not guaranteed to be collision-free. As of v0.11, the default hashing algorithm is `sha256`, which addresses collision risks." Corroborating local tree evidence (not a URL): `/tmp/kvsrc/vllm-main/vllm/config/cache.py:139` reads `enable_prefix_caching: bool = True`, i.e. prefix caching is on by default in the extracted 0.29-era tree, and `prefix_caching_hash_algo: PrefixCachingHashAlgo = "sha256"` at line 141.

And: "While there are many ways to implement prefix caching, vLLM chooses a hash-based approach." The doc specifies the key components and two hard constraints: "We only cache full blocks." And on hashing: "In previous versions, the hash key was not guaranteed to be collision-free. As of v0.11, the default hashing algorithm is `sha256`, which addresses collision risks." Corroborating local tree evidence (not a URL): `/tmp/kvsrc/vllm-main/vllm/config/cache.py:139` reads `enable_prefix_caching: bool = True`, i.e. prefix caching is on by default in the extracted 0.29-era tree, and `prefix_caching_hash_algo: PrefixCachingHashAlgo = "sha256"` at line 141.

title: Per-request `cache_salt` for prefix-cache isolation, hardened against DoS

fields.detail: The design doc documents salting as shipped: "By including a `cache_salt` in the request, this value is injected into the hash of the first block, ensuring that only requests with the same salt can reuse cached KV blocks. This prevents timing-based attacks where an adversary could infer cached content by observing latency differences. This offers protection without compromising performance." The mechanism is an extra hash component: "Extra hashes: Other values required to make this block unique, such as LoRA IDs, multi-modality input hashes (see the example below), and cache salts to isolate caches in multi-tenant environments." The parameter was later hardened by merged PR #54353 ("[Bugfix] Bound cache_salt length to prevent DoS via scheduler CPU exhaustion", merged 2026-08-30), whose body reads verbatim: "Adds `max_length=1024` to the `cache_salt` Pydantic `Field` on all six API protocol models: completions, chat completions, responses, pooling, Anthropic, and scale-out (token-in-token-out)." with the threat being an attacker able to send "arbitrarily large salt strings that are serialized via `pickle.dumps` + `sha256` on the single-threaded EngineCore scheduler, stalling all concurrent requests."

title: SGLang RadixAttention (canonical reference)

fields.detail: The canonical paper behind SGLang's radix-tree prefix reuse, retrieved from arXiv (submitted 12 Dec 2023, v2 6 Jun 2024). Verbatim from the abstract: "The runtime accelerates execution with novel optimizations like RadixAttention for KV cache reuse and compressed finite state machines for faster structured output decoding." Reported result, verbatim: "Experiments show that SGLang achieves up to 6.4x higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art inference systems on various large language and multi-modal models on tasks including agent control, logical reasoning, few-shot learning benchmarks, JSON decoding, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and multi-turn chat." This remains the reference implementation that later 2026 work (vLLM hybrid checkpoints, HiRadixTree, granularity papers) cites.

title: SGLang radix cache eviction policies (lru / lfu / slru / priority)

fields.detail: A shipped, documented eviction-policy surface for the radix cache, retrieved as clean markdown. Verbatim: "Select one with `--radix-eviction-policy`. All of them fall back to least-recently-used order within a tie." Policy semantics are documented per row, e.g. "`lfu` | The prefix with the fewest cache hits, then the least recent." and "`slru` | Prefixes still in the probationary segment, then the least recent within a segment." Two important scoping statements: "A policy only scores. It does not decide how much to free, and it cannot pin KV in memory — a node protected by the policy is still evicted if reclaiming everything else is not enough." and "`fifo`, `mru`, and `filo` also exist in the policy registry but are not offered on the command line. They are reachable only by out-of-tree code that extends the choice list, and exist for experiments rather than serving." The doc also states the tradeoff explicitly: "`lfu` and `slru` help when your traffic has a stable hot set that a recency-only policy keeps flushing; they hurt when prefix popularity shifts over time, because a prefix that earned a high hit count keeps its advantage after it stops being useful."

title: SGLang session-aware radix cache (soft-pinned KV per session)

fields.detail: Shipped multi-turn/agent KV retention feature. Verbatim: "This feature is implemented only by `UnifiedRadixCache`." Invocation: `SGLANG_ENABLE_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE=1 ... --enable-session-radix-cache`. Limits are documented up front: "Session references are soft protection, not memory pins. Referenced KV can still be evicted when reclaiming unreferenced KV is insufficient." Eviction order is spelled out per cache component, including hybrid ones: "Full attention | The reusable prefix path from the registered leaf to the root | Unreferenced nodes first, then referenced nodes with fewer session references, then the configured policy such as LRU" and "Mamba | The reusable state on the registered leaf | Two LRU passes: unreferenced nodes first, then referenced nodes if more space is required". Also: "UnifiedRadixCache still applies component cascade rules. Evicting an internal Full node also evicts its SWA and Mamba data; evicting SWA also evicts Mamba data; evicting Mamba affects only Mamba."

title: SGLang HiCache L3 cross-instance prefix sharing

fields.detail: This is the shipped answer to "can prefix KV be shared across instances". Verbatim tier statement: "L2 is node-local and instance-private." and "This is the answer to a common question: HiCache cannot pool the host memory of several machines into one larger L2. Growing `--hicache-ratio` or `--hicache-size` only makes each instance's own private L2 larger. Cross-instance reuse is the job of L3, so it needs `--hicache-storage-backend`." On the mechanism: "**Cross-instance Sharing**: When data is written back from L2 to L3, only data not already present in L3 is transferred. KV caches stored in L3 can then be shared across all SGLang instances in the cluster (depending on the L3 backend implementation), significantly improving cache hit rates within the same memory budget." Backends are enumerated verbatim: "Distributed backends such as `mooncake`, `hf3fs`, `nixl` and `aibrix` give cluster-wide scope, but only when every instance is pointed at the same namespace and configuration." The metadata structure is described as "HiRadixTree", extending RadixAttention: "HiRadixTree extends this idea: each node corresponds to the KV cache of a span of consecutive tokens and records where that KV cache is stored—whether in local GPU memory, CPU memory, L3 storage, or multiple of these tiers."

title: SGLang SMG router cache-aware routing policy

fields.detail: The shipped cache-aware routing policy, retrieved as markdown. Verbatim: "**Cache-Aware Policy (Default, Recommended)**" and "The cache-aware policy provides the best performance for most workloads". The mechanism list is verbatim: "1. Maintains an approximate radix tree for each worker based on request history 2. Routes requests to workers with the highest prefix match (cache hit) 3. Falls back to shortest-queue routing when load is imbalanced 4. Automatically evicts old entries to prevent memory overflow". Flags: `--policy cache_aware --cache-threshold 0.5 --balance-abs-threshold 32 --balance-rel-threshold 1.5 --eviction-interval-secs 120 --max-tree-size 67108864`. The same doc contrasts the non-router baseline: "No cache-aware routing", and reports "✅ Yes - significantly higher cache hit rate" for cache awareness, with an 8×A100 dp-size=8 benchmark attributed to the SGLang v0.4 blog.

title: vLLM internal prefill checkpoints for Mamba prefix caching (hybrid align mode)

fields.detail: Merged 2026-08-22 (state MERGED confirmed in the retrieved page payload). The problem statement is verbatim: "Mamba prefix caching currently splits a prefill at the last block boundary" with the before/after given as "Model forward (7680 tokens) -> FlashKDA(7680 tokens) -> save checkpoint -> Model forward (320 tokens) -> FlashKDA(320 tokens)" becoming "Model forward (8000 tokens) -> FlashKDA(7680) -> save checkpoint -> FlashKDA(320)". Benefit verbatim: "This PR helps us avoid a second full-model pass through attention, MoE, routing, and TP collectives." Title carries the measured result: "9%~25% TTFT improvement". Validation command uses `vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3 --trust-remote-code -tp 8 ... --enable-prefix-caching`. This answers "can a recurrent-state hybrid model actually get prefix-cache hits at all", and it supersedes the pre-existing state documented as open in the hybrid KV manager doc (see CLOSED-12).

title: vLLM hybrid prefix caching with spec-decode rewind and partial (sub-block) hits

fields.detail: Merged 2026-09-06. Verbatim purpose: "Extend the Kimi-K3 prefill checkpoint optimization from #52789 to support: speculative decoding / Eagle block rewind; partial prefix caching ( prefix_match_unit < Mamba block size ); and checkpoint blocks restored through KV connectors such as MooncakeStore." The correctness invariant is stated verbatim: "The cache manager and FlashKDA worker share the same checkpoint-validity rules, so a checkpoint block is allocated and hashed only when the worker can write it." Re-keying is described: "For an aligned partial checkpoint, the already reserved request-owned checkpoint block is re-keyed from its provisional boundary to the state position actually exported by FlashKDA. This PR keeps the block allocation, eviction, and free lifecycle introduced in #52789 ." Note that the validation hardware is TP8/EP8 across two 4-GPU nodes — the feature itself is not gated on it, but the reported numbers are.

title: vLLM fallback when a hybrid KV group cannot answer fine-grained lookups

fields.detail: Merged 2026-08-12. This is the shipped answer to the "fine-grained hits are silently disabled" failure mode. Verbatim summary: "Fine-grained prefix-cache hits are enabled for hybrid models containing Mamba `align` groups. However other groups, such as a sliding-window DSpark drafter, may use KV cache managers that only support block-aligned lookups. This previously caused an assertion when prefix caching was enabled." The change list: "Enables fine-grained hits only when every KV cache manager supports the required lookup granularity." / "Falls back to scheduler-block-aligned prefix hits for incompatible layouts." / "Prevents the scheduler from creating partial-tail cache entries after that fallback." / "Logs when fine-grained hits are disabled." The PR also documents its own cost verbatim: "Short and medium prompts may receive no prefix-cache reuse because hits must land on the much larger scheduler alignment." Reported result: "Repeated 66,007-token prompt reused 57,600 tokens."

title: vLLM retention interval for the offloading connector (prefix caching × KV offload × sliding window)

fields.detail: Merged 2026-09-04. Verbatim purpose: "Add retention interval support to `OffloadingConnector`. The Mooncake KV connector supports retention interval support via the `envs.VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL` env variable. It is used to avoid storing/loading blocks that are outside of the sliding window of the attention mechanism. This is implemented via block masks. The implementation in `OffloadingConnector` uses the same block mask mechanism to implement retention interval support." Test evidence is on gpt-oss-20b (a sliding-window hybrid) with `--enable-prefix-caching` and the CPUOffloadingSpec.

title: Hybrid KV Cache Manager (layer-type-specific prefix-cache rules)

fields.detail: The shipped design for making one block pool serve full-attention, sliding-window and Mamba groups with a single page size. Verbatim: "Support layer-specific prefix-cache rules, for example: Full attention: a cache hit prefix requires **all** tokens remain in the KV cache. Sliding window: a cache hit prefix only requires the last **`sliding_window_size`** tokens remain in the KV cache." The coordinator surface is named: `KVCacheCoordinatorNoPrefixCache`, `UnitaryKVCacheCoordinator`, `HybridKVCacheCoordinator`, with "Handles exactly two KV cache groups (must include one full‑attention group plus one other efficient‑attention group). Other cases are not implemented." Two candid limitations are in the doc itself: the overall banner "This feature is still in its early stage and things may change."; the grouping heuristic "This case happens in Gemma-3 series models... The solution has some memory waste and is not perfect."; and for Mamba, at the time of writing, "The prefix caching support of the mamba model is work in progress." (that last sentence is the pre-CLOSED-8 state; see also OPEN-4). ---

title: Where should the single retained recurrent-state checkpoint be placed in a hybrid model?

fields.who is still asking: nicholaskh-ai (vLLM), RFC #55697, with three follow-up PRs #55873 / #55875 / #55876 submitted for review
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "The core dilemma is that **from an engine-internal perspective, it is virtually impossible to heuristically predict where that single, high-value checkpoint boundary should be placed**. Geometry-based interval chopping frequently misses the actual shared premise or prematurely cuts across context. Conversely, **from the business application's perspective, this boundary is immediately obvious and trivial to locate** (e.g., precisely at the junction where a shared source item, document context, or system premise ends)."
fields.what specifically is missing: A decision on the mechanism (application-supplied `<|mamba_checkpoint|>` marker vs an engine heuristic), plus review of the three split PRs. title: Prefix-cache retention is one global scalar; hit-inert EAGLE sliding-window draft groups still spend the shared LRU

fields.who is still asking: vLLM contributor RFC #54661
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "On hybrid models that carry an EAGLE-style sliding-window draft group (DFlash/DSpark-shaped drafters), that group hashes `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) + 1` block ids at *every* prefix-cache boundary and frees them *cached* onto the protected tail of the one LRU that all groups share, while — once it is exempted from the hit `min` — contributing nothing to the reconciled hit length. On a GLM-5.3-Flash deployment this one group spends 87% of the prefix cache and caps coexisting conversations at ~50K tokens each."

The RFC also flags its own evidence status verbatim: "All numbers below are **deployment evidence from a vLLM fork**, not upstream verification".

title: Fine-grained (sub-block) prefix hits for sliding-window groups

fields.who is still asking: vLLM issue #53786 (filed against `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0` and re-verified on `main` @ 2026-08-25); a regression guard PR #54663 is open

title: Hybrid GDN prefix-cache hits can return NaN logits (correctness, not performance)

fields.who is still asking: vLLM bug report #55766 (v0.28.0, Qwen3.8-27B hybrid Gated-DeltaNet + attention, TP2 on 2x H100-80GB), open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Decode-produced boundary checkpoints are never prefix-cached in v0.28.0 (the running block is freed before `cache_blocks`), so only prefill chunk ends matter, which is consistent with the trigger being the prompt length. The Mamba/GDN checkpoint written when a prefill ends 4 to 10 tokens past a block boundary appears to be bad; a later request restores it from the prefix cache, produces NaN, and the NaN block is then itself cached, which is why the retry fails identically."

title: Hybrid mamba prefix-cache hit indexes the mamba block table in the wrong units

fields.who is still asking: vLLM bug report #55600, open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "`MambaHybridModelState.add_request` seeds the running mamba state slot as `(num_computed_tokens - 1) // self.cache_config.block_size`, but by the time it runs, `EngineCore._initialize_kv_caches` has already reassigned `cache_config.block_size` to `min(block_size of prefix-cacheable groups)`. For hybrid models that carry an extra attention group with a small block size (here: a DFlash2/EAGLE-style drafter group with sliding-window spec, block 64 or 1024), that minimum is far below `cache_config.mamba_block_size` (7168 here)." fields.what specifically is missing: A fix for the unit mismatch between `cache_config.block_size` (lowered to the smallest prefix-cacheable group) and `mamba_block_size`; the issue is open with no linked merged PR.

title: Prefix caching on Mamba-2/GDN hybrids produced 0% hits in v0.26.0 (silent no-op)

fields.who is still asking: vLLM issue #51250 (Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration), open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "On Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (architecture: Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration — a Mamba-2/GDN hybrid), enabling prefix caching (--enable-prefix-caching) results in 0% prefix-cache hits even for requests that share a long, identical prefix. The ask is explicit: "Preferably either: - vLLM should warn that --enable-prefix-caching is ineffective for hybrid SSM/Mamba models, or - vLLM should be extended to support caching the recurrent conv+SSM state so shared-prefix prefill reuse works for these hybrids."
fields.what specifically is missing: The issue is still open and self-labelled "Not re-verified on current main". Later merged work (CLOSED-8 / CLOSED-9) covers Kimi-K3/FlashKDA checkpoint paths, but no merged change tied to this issue was found, and the residual question — a general warning/telemetry for ineffective hybrid APC — remains open.

title: External/cross-instance KV connectors do not partition on `cache_salt`, so salting does not isolate them

fields.who is still asking: vLLM bug report #53495, open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "`ExampleConnector` derives its external storage key from the prompt token bytes only (`_generate_foldername_debug`, `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/example_connector.py:404-424`). `request.block_hashes` is never consulted, and `build_connector_meta` (`:299`, tokens only at `:315`) discards `new_req.lora_request`. So the dimensions that partition the in-engine prefix cache do not partition this connector: - Request A with `cache_salt="salt-x"` is stored. Request B with the same tokens and `cache_salt="salt-y"` gets `get_num_new_matched_tokens == 48`, three full blocks of A's KV."
fields.what specifically is missing: A connector-side key derivation that consumes `request.block_hashes` instead of re-deriving from tokens. The report generalizes the class explicitly: "This is the class in RFC #53194: a connector that re-derives its key from tokens instead of consuming `request.block_hashes` drops every dimension at once". A prior attempt on the HF3FS connector (#51640) was closed unmerged (see ABANDONED note) and the open re-attempt is #51748.

title: The `cache_salt` trust boundary and its efficiency cost are undocumented

fields.who is still asking: vLLM docs PR #53347, open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "**1. Where the salt must come from.** The merged text covers salt unpredictability but not its origin, and `cache_salt` is an ordinary request-body field. In a self-hosted deployment the caller writes it, so an adversary who sets their own salt to a victim's value recovers the shared blocks and the timing signal returns. Entropy does not help there — the adversary is not guessing the value, they are supplying it." And on measurement: "Measured on A100-SXM4-80GB with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct over a 2119-token shared prefix, read from `vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds`: 32.8 ms cached vs 149.6 ms uncached, about 4.6x."
fields.what specifically is missing: The doc addition itself is unmerged; the depth of the residual timing channel created by caller-supplied salts is not stated anywhere in the shipped docs.

title: The free list interleaves hit blocks with miss blocks, so hits are evicted before they can be reused

fields.who is still asking: vLLM PR #55998 by shanrow-amd, open

However we wish all hit blocks can be placed in the tail of the free list so that the hit blocks can be hit more and more before they are allocated out. So we introduce a new free list called hash-hit free list that is allocated after the original free list and to park hash-hit free blocks separately. title: Cache-aware admission ordering inside the engine (FCFS admission destroys pending cache hits)

fields.who is still asking: vLLM PR #54625 by fululi12, open
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Within a bounded look-ahead window over the waiting queue, admit requests whose prefix is already resident in the KV cache ahead of requests that would have to compute theirs. The problem is an interaction between strict FCFS admission and prefix caching: a cold request admitted first allocates blocks, and under pressure that allocation evicts blocks which a request further back in the queue still needs. The eviction turns a would-be cache hit into recomputation, and the deeper the shared prefix, the more expensive the loss." New flags are declared off by default: "Two new scheduler options, both off by default: Flag Default Meaning --cache-aware-admission-window N 0 Look-ahead depth over the waiting queue; 0 admits strictly in arrival order".
fields.what specifically is missing: A merge decision, and any published measurement. This is the same mechanism that was dropped in ABANDONED-1 ("A `CacheAffinityScheduler` plugin loadable via `--scheduler-cls` that reorders the V1 waiting queue by cached-prefix length before each scheduling iteration."), whose post-mortem measured +0.2%, so the open question is whether the new formulation clears the bar the old one missed. The sibling open PR #54366 "[Core] Add waiting-queue-informed KV cache eviction" addresses the eviction half.

title: Elastic KV cache built, measured, and reported as a negative result

fields.closure status: **published negative result** — the technique was built and explicitly judged not to pay off. This is the strongest "tried and given up" item in the paper literature for this subsection.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Having built the mechanism, we test the premise it rests on and report an honest negative result. It only pays off if a small prefill chunk size badly hurts prefill latency. In a controlled experiment injecting long prompts into a live decode load, that penalty is small (median time-to-first-token differs by about 1% between chunk sizes of 8192 and 32768 tokens), because prefill is compute bound and decode consumes only about one token per sequence per step. Simply lowering max_num_batched_tokens recovers more KV than the controller does, at nearly equal latency. The reserve also dilutes under tensor parallelism, from 16% of KV at TP1 to 2.7% at TP4."

title: External/NVMe prefix caching falls below break-even on a fast GPU

fields.who: Joseph Kanichai, Tiziano De Matteis, Animesh Trivedi — "Building py-kvcache: A Performance Characterization of External KV Caching for vLLM with NVMe SSDs"
fields.closure status: **published negative/limiting result** for the cross-tier and cross-instance direction on fast hardware; the authors recommend it be treated as a per-setup admission decision rather than a general win.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Prefix caching can reduce the time to first token (TTFT) of long-context LLM requests by reusing previously computed key-value (KV) states, but for short prefixes or fast GPUs, recomputation can be faster than loading from an external cache." And the decisive measurement, verbatim: "Bailian trace replays improve TTFT on a weaker GPU, but on an H100 the average request falls below the break-even point and GPU memory alone retains enough prefixes. External KV caching should therefore be treated as a setup specific admission decision."

title: Exact composition of all cached recurrent states for hybrid prefix reuse is unnecessary and can be harmful

fields.who: Yirui Liu, Ruoling Qi, Longwen Wang, Xuaner Wu, Jian Chen, Yuxin Jin, Jiawei Shao, Xuelong Li — "LinearKV"
fields.closure status: **published negative result** against a specific competing technique (exact state composition, attributed to concurrent work HYPIC) inside the hybrid prefix-caching design space; the paper argues the principled-looking approach does not pay off.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "The algebraically principled alternative---composing all $K$ cached states into the exact full-prefix state, as concurrent work HYPIC does---is unnecessary and, on some architectures, even harmful. We compare the two across three hybrid models and three PIC selectors. On the two GDN models the two tie, both recovering most of full quality (up to $92\%$); on the Mamba-2 model, exact composition instead collapses under every selector---under EPIC, for instance, it recovers only $46.6\%$ of full quality, versus $86.8\%$ for a single cached block initializer. A single state initializer is also cheaper, cutting time-to-first-token to $0.46\times$ full prefill versus a further $5$--$17\%$ overhead for exact composition".

title: Repairing reused KV for non-prefix positions is often worse than not reusing at all

fields.closure status: **published negative result** about the value of KV reuse outside the exact-prefix case, including a negative result for cache compression on agent reports and for trained adapters across checkpoints.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We find that correcting positions, which needs no recomputation, is enough until a question needs several sources at once. There, only methods that pay, by re-encoding part of the cache or by training, recover half to two thirds of the gap; unrepaired caches can be worse than no cache. Cache-compression methods that are harmless on a single prompt fall significantly behind position correction on freshly written agent reports." And: "When a different checkpoint wrote the cache, training-free methods are barely affected, while an adapter trained on one checkpoint's caches loses quality."

title: Cross-instance prefix sharing through a shared L3 tier (SGLang HiCache distributed backends)

fields.hardware requirement: more than one inference instance / a cluster-wide storage namespace; L2 is explicitly instance-private, so any cross-instance reuse needs a distributed L3 backend
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "**L2 is node-local and instance-private.** It is host memory owned by one inference instance's process, so two instances never read each other's L2, not even two instances on the same node. A KV cache produced by instance 0 becomes visible to instance 1 only after it reaches L3." And: "Distributed backends such as `mooncake`, `hf3fs`, `nixl` and `aibrix` give cluster-wide scope, but only when every instance is pointed at the same namespace and configuration." Also relevant to the single-GPU case: "The `file` backend writes to `/tmp/hicache` by default (`SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR` overrides it), which is node-local unless that path is a shared mount."

title: SGLang radix-cache eviction policy selection

fields.detail: SGLang ships a selectable prefix-cache eviction policy. Verbatim from the docs page: "Select one with `--radix-eviction-policy`. All of them fall back to least-recently-used order within a tie." The documented policy set is `lru` (default), `lfu`, `slru`, and `priority`, with the table row "slru | Prefixes still in the probationary segment, then the least recent within a segment. Like `lfu`, but you want a hard floor on how much a one-off prefix can displace a proven one." Parameterisation is shipped too: "Some policies take parameters. Pass them as a json object to `--radix-eviction-policy-config`". The page also names the shipped limits: "A policy only scores. It does not decide how much to free, and it cannot pin KV in memory — a node protected by the policy is still evicted if reclaiming everything else is not enough." and "Hit count (`lfu`, `slru`) counts how many times a node was matched by a later request. It is not incremented for chunked-prefill steps, for evicted nodes, or under write-back HiCache."

title: NVIDIA/kvpress — shipped eviction-method library

fields.detail: Verbatim from the README (retrieved from `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/kvpress/main/README.md`): "kvpress implements multiple KV cache compression methods and benchmarks using 🤗 transformers, aiming to simplify the development of new methods for researchers and developers in this field." The library ships implementations of essentially every method named in this subsection, e.g. "`SnapKVPress` ...: average attention weight of the last queries", "`StreamingLLMPress` ...: keep only the initial and recent tokens", "`PyramidKVPress` ...: maintain pyramid-like cache sizes, allocating more cache budget to lower layers and less to higher layers", "`AdaKVPress` ...: prune bottom scores of any `ScorerPress` but across all heads, achieving head-wise compressions", "`CriticalKVPress` and `CriticalAdaKVPress` ...: refine the scores using the L1 norm of Wo @ values, coupled with a two-stage selection.", and decoding-phase compression via `DecodingPress`. Install is a plain `pip install kvpress`.

title: Attention sinks are provably necessary (theory)

fields.detail: Verbatim from the abstract: "We prove that, in some settings, it is the latter: computing a trigger-conditional behavior necessarily induces a sink in softmax self-attention models." and "We also prove that non-normalized ReLU attention can solve the same task without any sink, confirming that the normalization constraint is the fundamental driver of sink behavior." This closes the question of whether the sink is merely an optimization artifact — a result relevant to any eviction policy that treats position-0 as a disposable token.

title: Recency/Frequency (ARC-style) adaptive KV block caching for vLLM

fields.detail: Verbatim from the abstract: "Existing cache management strategies adopt the least-recently-used policy for evicting cache blocks. However, LRU leads to multiple unrelated workloads flushing each other's caches. To address this, we integrate adaptive caching that dynamically allocates cache space between recently and frequently occurring KV blocks." Reported effect, verbatim: "it improves the KV cache hit rate by up to 10.8% and reduces time to first token by up to 12.6% over naive vLLM on synthetic document question answering workloads, and 2.1% and 2.0% respectively on real-world conversation workloads." Publication venue, verbatim: "Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM)". Note the small real-workload gains (2.1% / 2.0%) versus the 10.8% / 12.6% synthetic figures.

title: vLLM's GPU-side `BlockPool` has no policy knob at all — only a single LRU/FIFO free queue

fields.who is still asking: `sjmshsh` (author) in vLLM; issue state is `OPEN` with `"stateReason":"REOPENED"`, label `feature request`, created 2026-04-19, last updated 2026-08-21.
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "vLLM's GPU KV cache (`BlockPool`) uses a **single-queue LRU** implemented in`FreeKVCacheBlockQueue`. When a request finishes, its blocks are appended to the tail of the free queue. When new blocks are needed, eviction drains from the head. This design has one fundamental blind spot: **once `ref_cnt` drops to zero, all blocks are equal candidates for eviction, regardless of how many times they were previously reused.** A system-prompt block touched by 10,000 requests and a one-time-use block are indistinguishable at eviction time."
fields.verbatim quote, second part: "### The Inconsistency: CPU Offload Already Has ARC ... The GPU BlockPool has no equivalent. This RFC proposes closing that gap." Proposed API, verbatim: "Users who do not set \n- gpu_eviction_policy see identical behavior."
fields.what specifically is missing: no `gpu_eviction_policy` flag exists. Confirmed against the local vLLM tree: `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py` still holds exactly one `self.free_block_queue = FreeKVCacheBlockQueue(self.blocks)` and no policy registry; the pluggable `CachePolicyFactory` exists only under `vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/policies/` (offload tier), not for HBM blocks.

title: Eviction across replicated KV tiers has no principled policy (published open problem)

fields.who is still asking: the authors of "From Tensor Buffer to Distributed Memory Hierarchy: A Survey of KV Cache Management for LLM Serving" (arXiv 2607.02574), §6 design-gap agenda.
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "DG3—Eviction across replicated tiers. A KV block can be live in HBM, host DRAM, and a remote store simultaneously. Existing tier-aware systems often approximate this with per-tier heuristics. A principled policy would price each tier's fetch latency against the probability of near-future reuse, which requires per-block reuse-distance and lifetime traces. MG4 and MG5 are therefore prerequisites."
fields.verbatim quote of the measurement gap un: "Reuse-distance and block-lifetime distributions are also absent (MG4), which leaves eviction policies tuned by intuition rather than workload evidence."
fields.what specifically is missing: per-block reuse-distance and lifetime traces (MG4) and prefetchability slack (MG5); the survey states these are preconditions for the policy, not optional niceties.

title: Per-head sparse KV eviction (H2O-style) is not representable in vLLM's block manager

fields.who is still asking: a vLLM user asking on the official vLLM forum ("Sparse attention (e.g., H2O)", topic 2745, category KV-Cache). The thread contains the user's own partial workaround, which itself is the answer that the feature is missing.
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "I'd like to implement sparse attention KV cache policies (such as H2O) in vLLM. One issue I am running into is that a page (or block) needs to extend over all heads of a model. In H2O or other sparse attention methods, KV vectors can be in the cache for some heads, but not for others." and "Any pointer to how sparse attention can be properly implemented in vLLM, would probably help me. Or is this library simply restricted to serve non-sparse attention only?"
fields.verbatim quote of the answer given in-th: "vLLM currently assumes that KV cache blocks (pages) are allocated and managed at the sequence level, and all heads in a layer share the same block layout. This means that, as of now, vLLM does not natively support per-head or per-layer sparse KV cache eviction (such as H2O) where different heads could have different tokens retained in cache." The same post names the tracking RFCs: "[RFC]: Support KV Cache Compaction , RFC: Sparse KV cache management framework , and RFC: Support sparse KV cache framework" — all three of which are now closed or stale (see ABANDONED-1, ABANDONED-3, ABANDONED-4).
fields.what specifically is missing: a non-uniform KV memory layout across heads/layers. Directly stated by the RFC author in ABANDONED-1's thread: "If we want to support more advanced methods, we need a more flexible memory layout."

title: Score-based KV eviction selection signals — "the selection signal contributes almost nothing"

fields.who: authors of "Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning" (arXiv 2609.03430), submitted 2026-09-03.
fields.closure status: Published negative result against the whole scored-selection family (H2O/SnapKV/Ada-KV/TriAttention-style scoring).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We show that the selection signal contributes almost nothing. Random Attention keeps the prompt and evicts uniformly at random within each attention head, computing no score at all; across four models and six reasoning tasks it matches the strongest prior evictor while serving 32-43% higher throughput than it in vLLM deployment." Mechanism, VERBATIM: "1) the prompt is the fragile part of the cache, and most of the gap between selectors is just whether their selection signal happened to keep it; 2) the reasoning trace protects itself against eviction with redundancy at two levels, in the text (the model restates what it still needs as it works) and across attention heads (each keeps its own copy of the trace), so once the prompt is safe, a random draw retains enough copies of what the model still needs, and no score is required to pick them."

title: "Protection Is (Nearly) All You Need" — structural protection dominates scoring; H2O/SnapKV/StreamingLLM/Ada-KV/QUEST collapse without it

fields.who: authors of arXiv 2605.18053 (38 pages, code and figure regeneration scripts released), submitted 2026-05-18.
fields.closure status: Published negative result specifically about the score-based eviction policies named in this subsection.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Seven policies (LRU, H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, Ada-KV, QUEST, Random) share a prompt-boundary vulnerability: without structural protection, they collapse to near-zero quality on six pure-transformer models (F1$\leq$0.064)." and "With protection, simplified score-isolation variants are TOST-equivalent to LRU at $K{=}32$ ($\Delta{=}0.02$)". Overall conclusion, VERBATIM: "Overall: protection dominates; scoring differences are secondary once boundaries are guarded; per-head allocation gives a further modest gain." Its attention-mass measurement, VERBATIM: "the position-0 sink holds ${\sim}75\%$ of prefix mass, while other boundary tokens sit near ${\sim}0.41{\times}$ uniform expectation, so attention scorers retain the sink but still drop structurally critical tokens."

title: VarRate — SnapKV/Ada-KV style token selection collapses 11–15 points under query-agnostic reuse

fields.who: authors of "VarRate: Training-Free Variable-Rate KV Cache Compression for Long-Context LLMs" (arXiv 2607.15498), submitted 2026-07-16.
fields.closure status: Published negative result on irreversible eviction, specifically naming SnapKV and Ada-KV; the paper abandons eviction in favour of rank allocation.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Two leading training-free families are both structurally limited: token-selection methods (SnapKV, Ada-KV) score importance from an observation window and evict low-scoring tokens, but eviction is irreversible -- so when the importance signal degrades under query-agnostic reuse, accuracy collapses by 11-15 points; uniform low-rank coding keeps every token but spends equal rank everywhere, wasting budget. We observe that both failures share one cure: rank should be allocated, not evicted." Result, VERBATIM: "Because no token is dropped, it degrades by only 3.5-5.5 points where query-aware selection collapses."

title: "More GPUs or a Smaller Cache?" — no cost-equivalence crossover found; extra GPUs are largely wasted spend below a model-size wall

fields.closure status: Published negative result against the "add tensor parallelism instead of compressing the cache" answer to KV memory pressure.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We place tensor-parallel configurations (degree 1 to 8) and KV-compressed configurations (16/8/4-bit, keep-ratios down to 0.25) on one costnormalised axis, cost per million tokens against latency, using a profiled simulator calibrated on A100, A40, and H100 hardware, and we go looking for the cost-equivalence crossover. We do not find one. Across two models (Llama-2 at 7B and 70B), three GPU types, and every level of memory relief we could construct, compression is cheaper by 1.20x to 2.00x." Boundary, VERBATIM: "A 7B model on an 80 GB device cannot exhaust its KV budget within its own context window, and the boundary that decides between the strategies is model size relative to device memory, at roughly 36B parameters for an 80 GB card. Below that wall, compression dominates and extra GPUs are largely wasted spend". Counter-finding, VERBATIM: "Tensor parallelism is the only lever that improves latency (compression makes per-token latency worse, by 8 to 93%, through batching contention)".

title: "Move the Query, Not the Cache" — cross-instance MLA attention redistribution needs a multi-node H100 cluster with NVLink and InfiniBand/IBGDA

fields.hardware requirement: ≥2 nodes × 4 H100 SXM5, NVLink 4.0 intra-node, InfiniBand NDR-200 cross-node, NVSHMEM with IBGDA.
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Our primary platform is a production cluster of 4 × H100 SXM5 nodes, with direct all-to-all NVLink 4.0 intra-node (six bonded links per GPU pair, NV6 ; the 4-GPU HGX board carries no NVSwitch) and InfiniBand (NDR-200) cross-node, running NVSHMEM 26.3 with IBGDA enabled. A cross-instance run is a 2-node × 4-PE NVSHMEM job (PE 0 and PE 4 the cross-node pair)" Also, from the abstract: "We characterize cross-instance MLA attention on a real multi-node H100 cluster, distilling two reusable artifacts". The paper's premise is explicitly out-of-one-GPU: "When that corpus outgrows one GPU it is partitioned across instances, so a query and the blocks it selects often sit on different GPUs: answering it means attention across instances."

fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "AMD hardware affinity by design. UMBP explores software–hardware codesign opportunities with AMD GPU/CPU/NIC — examples include IBGDA and SDMA transports, AMD Infinity Storage (AIS), and GPU-initiated NVMe." and "The UMBP master is a cluster-wide KV placement directory covering all tiers (engine HBM, host DRAM, UMBP DRAM pool, SSD).
