title: FP8 e4m3 per-tensor KV cache, calibration-free (scale = 1.0), validated Hopper + Blackwell

fields.detail: vLLM's flagship FP8 KV-cache validation. The flag quantises both storage *and* the attention matmuls. Verbatim: "vLLM's --kv-cache-dtype fp8 flag quantizes the KV-cache and runs the entire attention computation (the QK and ScoreV matrix multiplications) in FP8 (e4m3 is the format used throughout this post)." On the calibration-free question the blog is explicit that scale=1.0 is the evaluated configuration: "Important: All evaluations use per-tensor uncalibrated quantization scales (i.e., scale = 1.0). This is the simplest possible configuration — no calibration data, no per-head tuning — and represents the worst-case scenario for accuracy." Headline result: "FP8 KV-cache and attention quantization introduces at most 1-2 points of accuracy degradation, with the lowest recovery at 97% (GPQA:Diamond, BF16 model)." Stated exceptions: "The main exceptions are workloads where prefill dominates on head_dim = 256 , hybrid models whose small sliding-window layers should be left in BF16, and models or backends that show persistent uncalibrated accuracy loss, where calibration remains important."

title: Per-token-head dynamic (calibration-free) INT8 / FP8 / INT4 KV scales shipped in vLLM 0.29.0

fields.detail: vLLM's `KVQuantMode` IntEnum enumerates the shipped modes with their scale granularity, verbatim: `INT8_PER_TOKEN_HEAD = 2  # per-token-head dynamic scales for int8`, `FP8_PER_TOKEN_HEAD = 3  # per-token-head dynamic scales for fp8`, `INT4_PER_TOKEN_HEAD = 4  # packed 2×int4/byte, RHT + asymmetric zp`, `NVFP4 = 5  # packed fp4 data + fp8 block scales`, and the four TurboQuant modes `TURBOQUANT_K8V4 = 6`, `TURBOQUANT_4BIT_NC = 7`, `TURBOQUANT_K3V4_NC = 8`, `TURBOQUANT_3BIT_NC = 9` documented as "Hadamard-rotated Lloyd-Max quant, packed K+V per slot." The runtime (not checkpoint) scale computation is logged from `vllm/config/cache.py`: "Dynamic per-token-head scales will be computed at runtime." The same file's non-per-token-head branch states the older caveat verbatim: "Meanwhile, it may cause accuracy drop without a proper scaling factor". This closes the per-token/per-channel-scale question for vLLM: KIVI-style asymmetry is now expressible without calibration.

fields.detail: Merged by tdoublep on Jun 24, 2026 ("tdoublep merged 72 commits into vllm-project:main"), merge commit `70749fd`. The PR body verbatim: "Based on PR: #40633 / Changed to only INT4_PER_TOKEN_HEAD". title: TurboQuant sub-4-bit online KV backend merged in vLLM (Hadamard rotation + Lloyd-Max)

fields.detail: Merged ("vllm-bot merged 10 commits into vllm-project:main"). Body verbatim: "TurboQuant adds online KV cache compression to vLLM's v1 attention backend using PolarQuant (WHT rotation + Lloyd-Max scalar quantization) for keys and uniform quantization for values. title: `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers` shipped — per-layer precision escape hatch

fields.detail: Merged; the flag is also documented in the vLLM FP8 KV-cache blog, verbatim: "We added --kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers ( vllm#33695 ) to allow for hybrid settings." The blog states the rationale verbatim: "Models like GPT-OSS use some layers with sliding window attention, where tokens attend to a fixed window size, for example 128 tokens. Here FP8 overheads cannot be amortized. Therefore, keeping those layers in BF16 is actually faster than quantizing them... Furthermore, if some layers are particularly sensitive to quantization, this feature allows skipping those layers." It is present in vLLM 0.29.0 source (`vllm/config/cache.py: kv_cache_dtype_skip_layers: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)`) and documented at https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.28.0/features/quantization/quantized_kvcache/ as accepting "either layer indices or layer-type names".

title: fp8_e5m2 KV cache unblocked for weight-only-quantised checkpoints

fields.detail: Merged by yewentao256 Jun 18, 2026. Body verbatim: "_init_kv_cache_quant rejects --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2 for every quantized checkpoint with \"fp8_e5m2 kv-cache is not supported with fp8 checkpoints\". But weight-only checkpoints (INT4/INT8 compressed-tensors, AWQ, GPTQ) carry no fp8 KV scales and are not fp8. On Ampere, where fp8_e5m2 is the only fp8 KV cache dtype that runs at all ( fp8_e4m3 is unsupported by the hardware), this makes fp8 KV cache unreachable for every weight-quantized model." This is the clearest shipped statement of the e4m3-vs-e5m2 hardware split: e5m2 is the Ampere-compatible format, e4m3 is not.

title: KIVI — per-channel K, per-token V, tuning-free 2-bit KV cache

fields.detail: The canonical answer to the per-channel/per-token scale question. Abstract verbatim: "Our findings indicate that the key cache should be quantized per-channel, i.e., group elements along the channel dimension and quantize them together. In contrast, the value cache should be quantized per-token. From this analysis, we developed a tuning-free 2bit KV cache quantization algorithm named KIVI." Also: "KIVI can enable Llama, Falcon, and Mistral models to maintain almost the same quality while using 2.6× less peak memory (including model weight)." Submission history shows v1 5 Feb 2024, v2 25 Jul 2024 (no 2025-2026 revision).

title: KVQuant — per-channel key quant, pre-RoPE key quant, non-uniform datatypes, per-vector dense-and-sparse outliers

fields.detail: The canonical reference for outlier handling in KV quantisation and the source of the "dense-and-sparse" idea. Abstract verbatim: "(i) Per-Channel Key Quantization, where we adjust the dimension along which we quantize the Key activations to better match the distribution; (ii) Pre-RoPE Key Quantization, where we quantize Key activations before the rotary positional embedding to mitigate its impact on quantization; (iii) Non-Uniform KV Cache Quantization, where we derive per-layer sensitivity-weighted non-uniform datatypes that better represent the distributions; and (iv) Per-Vector Dense-and-Sparse Quantization, where we isolate outliers separately for each vector to minimize skews in quantization ranges." Result verbatim: "we achieve < 0.1 perplexity degradation with 3-bit quantization on both Wikitext-2 and C4". Submission history runs to v6 on 28 May 2025.

title: TurboQuant — data-oblivious rotation + per-coordinate Lloyd-Max quantiser, near-optimal distortion

fields.detail: The theoretical paper underlying vLLM's shipped turboquant_* dtypes. Abstract verbatim: "TurboQuant achieves this by randomly rotating input vectors, inducing a concentrated Beta distribution on coordinates, and leveraging the near-independence property of distinct coordinates in high dimensions to simply apply optimal scalar quantizers per each coordinate." And: "Experimental results validate our theoretical findings, showing that for KV cache quantization, we achieve absolute quality neutrality with 3.5 bits per channel and marginal quality degradation with 2.5 bits per channel." The full HTML explains that the non-integer bit rates come from outlier splitting, verbatim: "These non-integer bit precisions result from our strategy of splitting channels into outlier and non-outlier sets, and applying two independent instances of TurboQuant to each, allocating higher bit precision to outliers." and "in our 2.5-bit setup, 32 outlier channels are quantized at 3 bits, while the remaining 96 channels use 2 bits, leading to an effective bit precision of ( 32 × 3 + 96 × 2 ) / 128 = 2.5". Note the paper's own setup is modest: "All experiments are performed using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU."

title: KVarN — calibration-free variance-normalised KV quantiser that targets autoregressive error accumulation

fields.detail: The most recent (Jun 2026) published answer to the "quantized-KV attention error" sub-question. Abstract verbatim: "KV-cache quantization can help improve this, but current methods are evaluated under prefill-like settings and errors behave differently under autoregressive decoding. We show that in the latter regime, quantization errors accumulate across timesteps, driven primarily by incorrect token scales. We introduce KVarN, a calibration-free KV-cache quantizer that applies a Hadamard rotation followed by a dual-scaling variance normalization across both axes of the K and V matrices." Claim verbatim: "KVarN establishes a new state-of-theart for KV-cache quantization on generative benchmarks, including MATH500, AIME24 and HumanEval, at 2-bit precision." A vLLM implementation is claimed available in the abstract.

title: FP8 long-context accuracy collapse traced to Tensor-Core accumulation precision, and fixed (two-level accumulation)

fields.detail: This is the strongest published entry on "quantized-KV attention error" as a *kernel numerics* problem rather than a storage-format problem. Verbatim: "Hopper's FP8 Tensor Cores are documented as accumulating into FP32 registers, but in practice the intermediate accumulation loses precision when the contraction dimension is large... When the contraction dimension reaches 100K or more, this imprecise accumulation causes drastic numerical errors. Concretely, in long context inference, during the Softmax(AttnScore) * V matmul, the contraction dimension corresponds to the context lengths. Empirically, we found that this can lead to accuracy regressions from 91% (BF16) to 13% (FP8) on a long-context needle-in-a-haystack task." The fix verbatim: "we added a two-level accumulation strategy (see SageAttention2 ) that writes the partially accumulated results into an actual FP32 register ( flash-attention#104 ), which brought the FP8 accuracy back to 89%." Residual cost verbatim: "On the downside, this two-level accumulation increases the register pressure and causes slowdowns during prefill... however, for head dimensions larger than 128, the prefill performance remains behind BF16."

Concretely, in long context inference, during the Softmax(AttnScore) * V matmul, the contraction dimension corresponds to the context lengths. Empirically, we found that this can lead to accuracy regressions from 91% (BF16) to 13% (FP8) on a long-context needle-in-a-haystack task." The fix verbatim: "we added a two-level accumulation strategy (see SageAttention2 ) that writes the partially accumulated results into an actual FP32 register ( flash-attention#104 ), which brought the FP8 accuracy back to 89%." Residual cost verbatim: "On the downside, this two-level accumulation increases the register pressure and causes slowdowns during prefill... however, for head dimensions larger than 128, the prefill performance remains behind BF16."

title: Is there a calibration-free sub-8-bit KV backend that does not lose throughput (KVarN)?

title: SGLang's FP8 KV-cache decode path is unfused and slower than BF16 at small batch / short context

fields.who is still asking: Swipe4057, SGLang issue #30815, OPEN since Jul 10, 2026
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "When enabling --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 on Hopper (H200, SM90) with the fa3 backend, decoding slows down compared to BF16 KV-cache, especially on small batches and short contexts. The slowdown is caused by runtime overhead that is absent on the BF16 path and that is not eliminated by a static FP8 checkpoint ." Root cause verbatim: "The root cause is architectural: sglang performs FP8 KV-cache quantization as a series of separate Python-level tensor operations (multiple kernel launches per layer per step), whereas the BF16 path is a single optimized store_cache call. On memory-bound decode with small batches, this overhead outweighs the 2× reduction in KV read traffic." The reporter quantifies it: "For a model with ~64 layers, this is 64+ × 3 = ~192 .to() launches per forward pass. Each .to() has ~2-5μs launch overhead → ~400-1000μs of pure launch overhead per decode step, comparable to the entire attention computation on small batches."
fields.what specifically is missing: A fused FP8 KV store kernel and a single central Q-quantisation point in SGLang, matching what vLLM already does. A related OPEN PR exists: "https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/31652" ("[JIT] Fuse FP8 KV-cache quantization into the store kernel", OPEN).

title: vLLM's own comprehensive evaluation concludes TurboQuant k8v4 is not worth using and the aggressive presets are unfit for production

fields.who: vLLM team (official vLLM blog, "A First Comprehensive Study of TurboQuant: Accuracy and Performance")
fields.closure status: published negative result from the project that shipped the technique — the maintainers' own recommendation is to prefer FP8 and avoid the aggressive presets
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "TurboQuant k8v4 does not provide any significant advantage over FP8. This TQ variant only provides modest KV-cache savings (2.4x vs 2x), which are not worth the consistent negative impact on throughput and latency metrics." And: "Avoid TurboQuant k3v4-nc and 3bit-nc without thorough validation. These aggressive variants can cause drastic accuracy drops that reach up to 20 points on challenging math and coding benchmarks. In addition to accuracy, their consistent performance degradation due to complex dequantization steps renders them unsuitable for production deployments." And the headline: "FP8 ( --kv-cache-dtype fp8 ) remains the best default for KV-cache quantization." Throughput verbatim: "All TurboQuant variants are strictly below BF16: on Qwen3-30B (Figure 9), ranging from 80% (k8v4) to 73% (3bit-nc)".

title: QAQ's own stated limitation — it needs attention scores that do not exist at quantisation time

fields.who: Cheng et al., the QAQ paper's own text (arXiv:2403.04643)
fields.closure status: self-declared limitation inside the paper, worked around with an assumption rather than solved
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Our quantization method necessitates the attention scores that quantify the degree to which future tokens attend to preceding tokens. However, these attention scores are not available at the time of quantization. To address this limitation, we invoke the persistence of importance theory, which posits that the attention scores ( i.e. , importance) of each token remain relatively constant ( i.e. , persistence) throughout the process of token generation."

title: TurboQuant's headline sub-4-bit compression does not survive contact with per-block metadata on a real 27B hybrid model

fields.who: a contributor running the TurboQuant × MTP correctness battery, in the ggml-org/llama.cpp discussion #20969
fields.closure status: measured shortfall against the advertised ratio, plus a demonstration that the freed memory is consumed by the speculative-decode draft branch
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "TurboQuant compresses KV by 2.75× at 256 K (16.00 → 5.81 GiB). The full-bit-rate ratio is ≈ 5×, but the per-block norms in turbo3 push effective bits/element to ≈ 6." And: "MTP roughly halves the practical ceiling on a 4090. Even with the smaller turbo3 KV (3.16 GiB at 136 K), TQ+MTP at 136 K is already at 24.02 GiB / 24.56 GiB total. The MTP draft branch's own buffers (compute, n_ubatch -scaled allocations) eat the headroom that TurboQuant freed up."

title: RFC — back-pressure detection for KV cache offloading tiers

fields.who is still asking: bnellnm, vLLM RFC issue #50031
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "vLLM's KV cache offloading framework (CPU DRAM, local NVMe, shared storage) does not detect or respond to bandwidth saturation on secondary tiers. When a tier is saturated — whether from concurrent eviction, excessive store operations, or high IOPS — the system continues dispatching load/store jobs that pile up, further degrading bandwidth for actual serving loads." and "**Saturated-Tier bottleneck: In the case when multiple secondary tiers are specified, all tiers receive the same amount of stores. The CPU blocks are protected from eviction, when the stores are in progress and are released only when the slowest tier has completed the store. Here the slowest tier becomes the bottleneck for the entire system. Further, we observe CPU tier running out of memory, preventing further offloads."
fields.what specifically is missing: The RFC states its own scope limit verbatim: "The initial implementation adds back-pressure detection to secondary offloading tiers and a single response policy: drop store (write) requests to a tier that is under pressure. No load prioritization, tier rerouting, or load-vs-recompute decision is included in this phase." So load prioritization, tier rerouting, and any load-vs-recompute decision remain unsolved.

title: Unread tiered promotions are evicted by other speculative promotions (open PR, unfixed)

fields.who is still asking: AlejandroParedesLT, vLLM PR #50014 (open, fixes #49902)
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "TieringOffloadingManager promotes secondary-tier blocks to the primary CPU tier on every lookup() , including probes for waiting requests the scheduler ends up skipping that step (a request that defers is continue d past, not break ed on, so one schedule() pass can walk the whole waiting queue and issue a promotion per secondary-tier hit). Under many concurrent, disjoint-working-set requests, one promotion's landed-but-not-yet-GPU-read block could be evicted by another promotion before ever being consumed ... The evicted data gets re-promoted (and re-evicted) on a later step, burning secondary-tier I/O on data that never gets used."
fields.what specifically is missing: The fix (track landed-but-unread promotions and protect them) is proposed but the PR is still open — the shipping tiering manager has no protection for in-flight promotions.

title: SGLang HiCache never consults L3 when a prefix survives only as backuped stubs after host-tier eviction

title: LMCache does not decouple KV cache management from the inference engine, and cannot host token-dropping research

fields.who is still asking: the LMCache authors, in their own paper's deployment-lessons section
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Many storage companies, such as company I, R, C, and W, have explicitly asked for decoupling the KV cache management and the core inference code, since they want to touch as minimum core inference logic as possible. Although LMCache does not solve this for now, the trend is clear: an LLM inference engine is pairing with a variety of external KV cache management services." Second limitation verbatim: "As a concrete example, a rich set of research literatures explore dropping tokens from KV cache for compressing it into smaller tensors. However, it is non-trivial to implement token dropping in LMCache , since LMCache assumes the number of tokens that is input to and output of LMCache should be the same. Furthermore, any intermediate states in the attention module are hidden from the LMCache 's side, so research works that need to access or modify the attention states are hard to be implemented with LMCache ."
fields.what specifically is missing: (a) a clean engine/cache-engine separation interface; (b) any ability for the cache layer to change the token count or touch attention intermediates, which blocks token-dropping/compression research from being expressed in the cache layer.

title: Direct GPU↔storage access (GPU Direct Storage / GPU-GPU) is explicitly NOT intended to be supported in vLLM's tiering design

fields.stated reason, verbatim: The RFC carries a section headed "What we don't intend to support", whose two bullets read verbatim: "Direct GPU access (neither GPU-storage or GPU-GPU communication)" and "Limited flexibility for variance in block size. While we allow vLLM block size to vary, CPU block size must be constant across all vLLM nodes (and a multiple of the underlying vLLM block size)." The shipped doc restates the first bullet verbatim: "Only the CPU primary tier has direct GPU access. Secondary tiers cannot read from or write to GPU memory; all GPU↔secondary transfers are staged through the CPU primary tier."

title: External NVMe KV caching yielded no TTFT benefit on a fast GPU with large VRAM (break-even not reached)

fields.who: t348575 et al., py-kvcache (arXiv 2609.11744), §7 and conclusion
fields.closure status: the paper's own conclusion undercuts unconditional external caching — "External KV caching should therefore be treated a setup specific admission decision"
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "The same traces show a different outcome on the Snellius node. Their average request length is below the measured 6,203 token SSD break-even point for Qwen3 4B, on our setup, and the H100's larger GPU memory retains a large portion of the working set. As a result the TTFT of only using GPU prefix caching is identical to that of py-kvcache , while the native vLLM KV Offload implementation is 0.2 s higher." and "Below roughly 8k tokens the prefill is short enough that no storage device we measured can load the prompt faster than the GPU rebuilds it, and on a mid-range drive that threshold moves out to 32k. Therefore, external cache admission must depend on the model, GPU, SSD, and reusable prefix length rather than treating every hit as beneficial."

title: KV offloading degrades accuracy on context-intensive tasks

fields.who: Yandex authors, "KV Cache Offloading for Context-Intensive Tasks" (arXiv 2604.08426)
fields.closure status: negative empirical result in a published paper — offloading caused "significant performance degradation"; the authors nonetheless argue the technique is salvageable
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We evaluate modern KV offloading on Text2JSON and other context-intensive tasks and find significant performance degradation on both Llama 3 and Qwen 3 models. Our analysis identifies two key reasons for poor accuracy: low-rank projection of keys and unreliable landmarks." Second bounded result verbatim: "Our observations suggest that some model-benchmark pairs require very large budgets (over 10%) to achieve near-lossless accuracy." The authors do NOT declare the technique dead — verbatim: "These are not conceptual problems with the offloading itself, but technical limitations that can be circumvented with better compression and key selection. Our 'view from trenches' shows that KV offloading is still a good candidate for production use across both easy and context-intensive tasks."

title: KV offload to host DRAM is memory-bound by construction on typical workloads

fields.who: authors of "Understanding Bottlenecks for Efficiently Serving LLM Inference With KV Offloading" (arXiv 2601.19910)
fields.closure status: negative analytic + empirical result in a published paper — the paper's central finding is that typical workloads sit far past the memory-bound threshold
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "KV cache offloading enables long-context LLM inference by storing caches in CPU DRAM, but PCIe bandwidth limitations create severe bottlenecks. In this paper, we develops an analytical framework that derives κ_crit, the critical cached-to-prefill token ratio where execution becomes memory-bound and show typical workloads exceed this threshold by orders of magnitude. Empirical characterization reveals 99% of latency spent on transfers and serving offloaded requests results in GPU's consuming only 28% of their rated TDP, motivating our proposed optimizations for hardware interconnects, model architectures, and scheduling algorithms." Supporting figure verbatim (body §2.3, delegated retrieval): "HBM, tightly integrated on a silicon interposer, delivers TB/s, while CPU-GPU PCIe 5.0 provides only 64 GB/s—2% of HBM's bandwidth. Transferring a 50 GB KV cache takes 15 ms from HBM but 800 ms from CPU DRAM."

title: HERALD's own measurement — host-memory KV fetch overtakes the forward pass at 8K context

fields.closure status: the paper's own negative characterization of the PCIe tier, which is why it abandons per-step full-cache fetching

This gap widens drastically as the sequence extends, reaching 7.61x at 32K context. Even with a hypothetically perfect overlap of communication and computation, the per-step latency would still be limited by max(forward, fetch)."

title: HiCache host-memory sizing guard (`host_memory_budget_bytes`)

fields.hardware requirement: multiple co-located ranks on one host (demonstrated at `--tp 8`); the guard divides free RAM by `ranks_per_host()`, so the double-charging bug cannot occur with a single rank
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Splitting the free memory by the number of co-located ranks is only right for a reading taken before any of those ranks allocates. But each rank reads available at the moment it reaches the guard, and TP ranks reach it at different times: pinning a large host pool takes seconds and nothing synchronizes the ranks between pools. A rank that arrives after k peers have already pinned their pools sees available reduced by k × pool while still dividing by the full rank count, so the peers' pools are subtracted twice and the guard raises ValueError: Not enough host memory available on a host that has room for all of them." The reproduction is stated as "Any multi-GPU host. Size the pools so that all of them fit together but each per-rank guard has little slack, e.g. for 8 ranks ... --hicache-size <N>".

title: MiniCache

fields.detail: Depth-dimension KV merging, the technique that most "KV merging" papers build on. Verbatim: "we present a simple yet effective approach, called MiniCache, to compress the KV cache across layers from a novel depth perspective, significantly reducing the memory footprint for LLM inference. Our approach is based on the observation that KV cache states exhibit high similarity between the adjacent layers in the middle-to-deep portion of LLMs. To facilitate merging, we propose disentangling the states into the magnitude and direction components, interpolating the directions of the state vectors while preserving their lengths unchanged."

title: CommonKV (training-free cross-layer KV compression by adjacent-parameter SVD sharing)

fields.detail: Verbatim: "we propose CommonKV, a training-free method for cross-layer KV cache compression through adjacent parameters sharing. Inspired by the high similarity observed in cross-layer hidden states, we utilize Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to achieve weight sharing across adjacent parameters, resulting in a more easily mergeable latent KV cache." and "By integrating these approaches, we can ultimately achieve a 98\% compression ratio without significant performance loss."

title: Why can a NoPE MLA model not be served at all on SM120 across every SGLang DSA backend?

fields.who is still asking: fsadj, SGLang issue #39302
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "On **SM120** (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0) this model cannot be served at all. Every `--dsa-prefill-backend` / `--dsa-decode-backend` choice fails, each for a distinct reason, and the one backend the code *forces* for GLM + fp8 KV + SM120 is the one whose FlashInfer kernel rejects NoPE. So with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` the model is unrunnable by construction".
fields.what specifically is missing: shared-memory budget. The reporter measured `cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlockOptin` = "101376 B (99 KB)" on this part versus "Hopper/B200 expose ~228 KB, which is the budget the kernels below are written against", so the tilelang sparse-MLA prefill kernel's 202 KB demand cannot be satisfied. Page badge shows label "Open". Reported 2026-09-13 with SGLang 0.5.19, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB — i.e. exactly the target configuration.

title: Can attention run directly on low-rank/Tucker factors without materializing the KV cache at decode?

fields.who is still asking: the JoLT authors, in their own systems-direction statement
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Decode reconstructs the compressed cache from its Tucker factors at each step, an arithmetic cost that today's attention kernels are not built to absorb; a fused kernel that runs attention directly on the factors, without materializing the cache, is the natural route to decode parity and the main systems direction we leave open."
fields.what specifically is missing: a fused decode kernel that consumes the factored representation in place of a materialized cache; the paper reports only a FastJoLT compression-time speedup and leaves decode parity unbuilt.

title: Can a smaller unconstrained set of KV pairs be *learned* (rather than selected or merged) to preserve attention behaviour?

fields.who is still asking: the KVSculpt authors, positioning against both eviction and merging
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Along the sequence-length dimension, existing methods range from pure eviction -- selecting which KV pairs to keep -- to merging, which combines similar pairs into fewer ones. Both remain anchored to the original cache entries. We propose KVSculpt, which moves to the other end of this spectrum: instead of selecting or combining original pairs, we optimize a smaller set of unconstrained KV pairs in continuous embedding space to preserve each layer's attention behavior."

title: MLA's absorbed form for *training* — hard-banned by Megatron-Core, and measured to be a memory loss

fields.who: Megatron-Core (NVIDIA) as the abandoner; the LAGA authors as the measurers
fields.closure status: "by design" — a hard assertion in shipped library code disables the technique, with no documented reason; the paper explains the ban is well-founded.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Open Megatron-Core's MLA implementation NVIDIA (2025) and the forward begins with an assertion that bans its own low-communication path from training: assert not (self.training and self.cache_mla_latents). The absorb reformulation — folding kv_b_proj into the query so attention runs against the compressed latent and only the small latent crosses the collective — is fully implemented in the class, but gated to is_decode_only() inference and hard-asserted out of training. The library ships no low-communication MLA training path". Additional verbatim: "MCore's designers deliberately restrict the absorb trick to inference: the class's prepare_for_absorption even concedes that it is \"not doing true absorption. We will add this support at a later time.\" One contribution of this paper (§3.2/4.3) is to explain why that restriction is well-founded — the absorbed form, ported to training, regresses activation memory by 20–34% (up to 9.2 GB at V3 scale)". Also verbatim from the paper's own limitations: "Why this is both comm-cheap and memory-neutral. ... Measured: Laga peak memory matches B1 within ≤0.5% (<27 MB) while B2 balloons by up to 9.2 GB (Table 2)."

The absorb reformulation — folding kv_b_proj into the query so attention runs against the compressed latent and only the small latent crosses the collective — is fully implemented in the class, but gated to is_decode_only() inference and hard-asserted out of training. The library ships no low-communication MLA training path". Additional verbatim: "MCore's designers deliberately restrict the absorb trick to inference: the class's prepare_for_absorption even concedes that it is \"not doing true absorption. We will add this support at a later time.\" One contribution of this paper (§3.2/4.3) is to explain why that restriction is well-founded — the absorbed form, ported to training, regresses activation memory by 20–34% (up to 9.2 GB at V3 scale)". Also verbatim from the paper's own limitations: "Why this is both comm-cheap and memory-neutral. ... Measured: Laga peak memory matches B1 within ≤0.5% (<27 MB) while B2 balloons by up to 9.2 GB (Table 2)."
- Date: submitted 20 Jul 2026 (v1).
- Evidence: READ BODY

title: SVD/low-rank compression of attention projections — found to *accelerate* rank collapse on pretrained models (negative result)

fields.closure status: paper reporting an explicitly negative original finding that undercuts the standard motivation for SVD-based KV/attention projection compression.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "we report an original finding that using SVD compression of attention projections actually has the opposite effect on the rank collapse of the network: while it strongly suppresses it at initialization, it accelerates on pretrained models (for GPT-2 124M, GPT-2 Medium 355M, and Pythia-160M) with minimal risk of object aliasing artifacts appearing (verified on all compression ratios) and is consistent across four rank estimation methods." The paper also states the problem framing verbatim: "Section VI identifies an open question the reviewed literature does not address: whether the compression methods of Sections III-B through III-D compound with, or counteract, the network's natural tendency toward rank collapse. ... The two regimes produce opposite answers."

title: Pure low-rank (Tucker/SVD) KV backbones — insufficient on the value spectrum; degrade sharply past ~4x

fields.who: the JoLT authors, reporting their own ablation against the pure-low-rank alternative
fields.closure status: paper finding that the low-rank-only variant of the technique does NOT pay off (requires a quantized residual to become near-lossless), and that downstream quality collapses past a threshold.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "A pure low-rank backbone cannot reach near-lossless fidelity on its own, because truncation discards real energy, and on the flat value spectrum that energy is large. The residual recovers it." Additional verbatim: "Mistral degrades gracefully, losing roughly 4% perplexity per integer ratio step from 4× on, whereas LLaMA degrades sharply between 4× and 5×. We return to this split repeatedly, because it is the main caveat on an otherwise architecture-agnostic result." and "LLaMA GSM8K falls to 18.5%, 6.0%, and 1.5% at 4×, 6×, and 8× (Appendix F), the downstream face of its perplexity degradation". Also verbatim on the competing family: "A two-dimensional factorization must commit to one axis of redundancy and ignore the others, and a fixed-bit-width quantizer cannot reach the modest, intermediate compression ratios where quality is still free, because its smallest setting already overshoots them."

title: Low-rank KV compression on the target model class — keys compress, values do not; Qwen3-4B is the sensitive case

fields.who: the KV-CoRE authors (benchmark paper, 5 domains / 16 languages)
fields.closure status: benchmark finding that limits low-rank KV compression and specifically flags the target researcher's model as the fragile one.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Keys are consistently more compressible than values." and "We evaluate the performance degradation of compressed models using both perplexity (PPL) and GPT-score. Figure 3 presents PPL heatmaps of Qwen3-4B and LLaMA-2-7B on the Alpaca dataset across a grid of KV-cache compression ratios ... We can see that LLaMA-2-7B remains relatively stable, showing only modest PPL increases even under aggressive compression, whereas Qwen3-4B is more sensitive, exhibiting substantial degradation." Also verbatim on why uniform compression fails: "This heterogeneity indicates that future KV-cache compression should be layer-aware: applying a uniform compression ratio risks overly degrading high-rank layers while missing opportunities for more aggressive reduction in lower-rank ones."

title: Post-training SVD of projection weights for KV savings — achievable compression is bounded and Q/K joint compression is catastrophic

fields.closure status: paper concluding the retraining-free variant of the technique does NOT pay off beyond moderate ratios, and that the obvious stronger form destroys the model.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Table 5 reveals a striking asymmetry. Compressing both W_Q and W_K is catastrophic—at rank 192, errors in Q and K compound through the softmax, producing a cross-term Δ_Q Δ_K^⊤ that destroys attention patterns. However, compressing K alone is far more forgiving: rank 384 (d_model/2) incurs only 2.0% degradation." and "Post-training SVD of W_K alone provides a viable, retraining-free path to moderate KV cache savings. However, the achievable compression is limited: K-only SVD at d_model/4 (rank 192) degrades by 26%, whereas training from scratch with d_select=d_model/4 costs only 4.3% on WikiText-103."

title: MLA's shipped "MQA-absorb-only" decoding design — does not pay off off-H100 (hardware coupling)

fields.who: the GQLA authors, analysing the deployed MLA design
fields.closure status: paper concluding that the *shipped* MLA decode path is a regression relative to its own goals on non-H100 hardware; proposes replacing it.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "We identify three coupled hardware drawbacks of MLA's MQA-absorb-only design: hardware coupling to H100, loss of head-axis tensor parallelism, and zero MTP gain on commodity inference GPUs." and "On the NVIDIA H100, whose BF16 roofline (Williams et al., 2009) ridges around 295 FLOPs/byte, the absorbed MQA path with the canonical configuration ... and single-token decoding lands its arithmetic intensity at ≈242 FLOPs/byte, just below the ridge. This perfect H100 fit, however, is the only operating point MLA exposes."

title: NixlPushConnector — push-mode cross-instance KV transfer

fields.detail: Verbatim: "The default NIXL connector is **pull-based**: the decode (D) instance reads KV blocks from the prefill (P) instance via `NIXL READ` after prefill completes. `NixlPushConnector` adds a **push-based** alternative in which P writes the KV blocks directly into D's pre-allocated memory via `NIXL WRITE`." The doc also specifies the dedicated per-TP-rank background thread: "``NixlPushConnectorWorker`` introduces a single dedicated background thread per worker (i.e. per TP rank), named ``nixl-push-writer``." This is a shipped connector name (`"NixlPushConnector"` in the factory registry).

title: Mooncake Store Connector heterogeneous-TP KV sharing

fields.detail: The tracked problem and the merged fix are stated by the RFC author, z-zanez, in vLLM issue #55598 (retrieved): "Mooncake Store originally tied object keys and payload layout to the local TP rank. Two vLLM instances using the same model but different TP sizes therefore produced different shard counts, KV-head ranges, and namespaces and could not reuse each other's persisted KV cache." The fix: "[KV Connector] Support heterogeneous TP sharing in Mooncake Store Connector #53129 adds a common Store TP layout for Full Attention. Local TP ranks map to stable Store shards, allowing supported TP4/TP2/TP1 instances and multiple Prefill TP sizes to reuse and update the same Store entries." All three PR pages display the merged badge. PR #53129 title as retrieved: "[KV Connector] Support heterogeneous TP sharing in Mooncake Store Connector by z-zanez".

fields.detail: Verbatim: "The P2P tier (`type: "p2p"`) shares completed KV blocks between vLLM instances over RDMA via NIXL. title: Cross-process KV cache key determinism (dedup across instances)

fields.detail: Verbatim: "KV cache sharing between multiple vLLM instances using the same `root_dir` (e.g., via a shared PVC) works by default: `NONE_HASH` (the chain-hash seed for block content hashes) is derived from a fixed default seed, so identical token content produces identical block filenames across instances. To use a custom shared seed instead, set the `PYTHONHASHSEED` environment variable to the same value on every instance." The documented exception is also stated verbatim: "The exception is the non-cryptographic `xxhash` and `xxhash_cbor` values of `--prefix-caching-hash-algo`, which seed `NONE_HASH` randomly per process so the seed stays unpredictable."

title: NIXL KV cache lease renewal

fields.detail: Verbatim: "The lease renewal mechanism addresses both problems simultaneously. P grants a **short initial lease** (default 30s) when prefill completes. While a request is **queued or in-flight** on D, D **periodically sends heartbeats** to P extending the lease." The doc attributes the mechanism: "This mechanism was introduced in [PR #41383](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41383)." (PR #41383 itself was not fetched — cited only as quoted text inside this retrieved doc.) Also verbatim on the transport-agnostic heartbeat: "The notification medium is backend-specific, with automatic fallback from IB/RoCE to TCP already handled by NIXL."

title: SGLang HiCache — hierarchical KV with cross-instance L3 sharing

fields.detail: Verbatim: "Inspired by the classic three-level cache design of modern CPUs, HiCache organizes GPU memory as L1, host memory as L2, and distributed storage as L3." and "When data is written back from L2 to L3, only data not already present in L3 is transferred. KV caches stored in L3 can then be shared across all SGLang instances in the cluster (depending on the L3 backend implementation)". The available L3 backends are stated verbatim: "Distributed backends such as mooncake , hf3fs , nixl and aibrix give cluster-wide scope, but only when every instance is pointed at the same namespace and configuration."

title: Race-free KV-event endpoint discovery across data-parallel ranks

fields.who is still asking: touch869 (vLLM), feature request, opened 2026-09-07
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Today a consumer of KV events across data-parallel ranks has no race-free way to know where each rank's publisher landed" and "There is no Python/HTTP query surface." The issue proposes "a read-only GET /kv_event_sources route (mounted unconditionally, like the lora/tokenize routers — not behind VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE ) plus an AsyncLLM.get_kv_event_sources() method".
fields.what specifically is missing: bind-time ephemeral port allocation (`tcp://*:0` currently "degenerates to literal ports 0,1,2,... — rank ≥ 1 binds privileged/invalid ports"), endpoint readback via `zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT`, and the discovery API. The issue states the workaround in place today: "ZmqEventPublisher._socket_setup() binds the socket but never reads back the assigned port ( zmq.LAST_ENDPOINT ), so with :0 the OS-assigned port is silently discarded".

title: Chunked prefill is the default V1 scheduler behaviour

fields.detail: vLLM docs state the feature is shipped and on by default, and that a request exceeding the token budget is automatically split: "In V1, chunked prefill is enabled by default whenever possible . With chunked prefill enabled, the scheduling policy prioritizes decode requests." and "If a pending prefill request cannot fit into max_num_batched_tokens , it automatically chunks it." The same page gives the long-context tuning rule: "For optimal throughput, we recommend setting max_num_batched_tokens > 8192 especially for smaller models on large GPUs." Cross-checked in the local tree: `vllm/config/scheduler.py:116` declares `enable_chunked_prefill: bool = True` and `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py` `_set_default_chunked_prefill_and_prefix_caching_args` sets `self.enable_chunked_prefill = default_chunked_prefill` when the user passes nothing.

title: `--long-prefill-token-threshold` caps how much of a long prompt one chunk may take

fields.detail: The flag is shipped and is read from the local source tree. `vllm/config/scheduler.py:70-72` declares `long_prefill_token_threshold: int = Field(default=0, ge=0)` with the docstring "For chunked prefill, a request is considered long if the prompt is longer than this number of tokens. 0 disables the cap (default)." It is registered as `--long-prefill-token-threshold` at `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:1596` and consumed in the scheduler at `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:663` (`if 0 < self.scheduler_config.long_prefill_token_threshold < num_new_tokens:`), with `long_prefill_threshold` also read at `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:476`. Startup validation rejects a value above the model window (`vllm/config/scheduler.py:324-329`): "long_prefill_token_threshold ({self.long_prefill_token_threshold}) cannot be greater than the max_model_len ({max_model_len})." The flag is exercised by in-tree tests, e.g. `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:608` (`long_prefill_token_threshold=400`) and `tests/v1/core/prefix_cache/test_partial_prefix_cache_hits.py:271`. Caveat recorded separately as OPEN-6: this flag's interaction with long-context chunked prefill is still producing user-visible corruption reports.

title: Sub-block prefix-cache matching for long shared system prompts

fields.detail: This is the direct answer to system-prompt cache bloat on hybrid checkpoints. The doc states the workload and the fix: "This helps when many requests share a long system prompt and then diverge. It is off by default, and takes effect only when all of the following hold" — followed by the four required conditions (`--mamba-cache-mode align`, EAGLE/MTP speculative decoding on the Mamba group, `--prefix-match-unit` smaller than the Mamba block size, no multi-module MTP). The matching-granularity knob is documented in-tree at `vllm/config/cache.py:100-109`: "The finest token boundary (in tokens) a prefix-cache hit can land on. … It can be set finer than the physical KV cache block sizes (e.g. 32 vs a 1024-token hybrid-model block) as long as every KV cache group's `block_size` is divisible by it, enabling cache hits at boundaries inside a physical block."

title: Decode context parallelism (KV sharded along T) is shipped in vLLM

fields.detail: The in-tree deployment doc defines the feature and its bound: "Since `H` is limited (determined by the model architecture), when we continue to increase the tensor parallel size, the KV cache for each GPU will be duplicated for `tp_size / H` times. … Then we need to add decode context parallel to further shard the KV cache along the `T` dimension. This is as simple as adding `-dcp <size>` to the command line." and "The dcp size should lie in the range of `[1, tp_size/H]`." The doc also states the status of the *prefill* half honestly: "Both approaches are under active development." Flags are registered in `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:1090-1115` (`-dcp`, `--dcp-comm-backend`, `--dcp-q-replicate`, `--dcp-kv-cache-interleave-size`, `-pcp`). The interleaving sharding scheme is attributed to a named contributor and a paper: "This is proposed by [Chao Hong from Moonshot](https://github.com/youzhedian), and also explained in details in [this paper](http://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07120)." That linked paper resolves to "[2507.07120] Helix Parallelism: Rethinking Sharding Strategies for Interactive Multi-Million-Token LLM Decoding" (verified by fetching the abs page).

title: Prefill context parallelism is shipped in SGLang with two selectable sharding layouts

fields.detail: The server-arguments reference lists the live flags and their semantics verbatim: "`--enable-prefill-cp` — Enable context parallelism for the prefill phase. (default False, "bool flag (set to enable)") and "`--cp-strategy` — Sharding strategy for prefill CP. zigzag assigns each rank one early and one late sequence block; interleave assigns token indices modulo the CP size." (choices `zigzag , interleave`, default None). fields.detail: The merge event is on the page: "AndreasKaratzas merged 7 commits into main vllm-project/vllm:main from akaratza_rocm_aiter_mla_sinks … Sep 7, 2026". title: Cartridges at Scale — pre-encoded KV for large document collections

fields.detail: Retrieved abstract (title "[2606.04557] Cartridges at Scale: Training Modular KV Caches over Large Document Collections", submitted 3 Jun 2026): "Large Language Models can reason over long contexts, yet prefilling millions of tokens is wasteful as much of the content remains static across queries. Cartridges address this by distilling document collections into reusable key-value (KV) caches that eliminate prefilling while preserving accuracy." The paper also closes the specific failure it inherited: "A critical limitation of this approach is that cartridges are monolithic and non-compositional: encoding an entire collection into a single KV block does not scale, and naively mixing cartridges trained in isolation collapses performance to near chance." Its own limitations section keeps the scope honest (see ABANDONED-5 for the inverted-negative reading of the same text).

title: VPP — a published fix for chunk-count-induced prefill fragmentation

fields.detail: Retrieved abstract (title "[2608.26523] VPP: Virtual Pipeline Parallelism for Efficient Chunked Prefill in Long-Context LLM Inference", submitted 27 Aug 2026): "Existing approaches mitigate this imbalance through dynamic chunk resizing (Dynamic CPP, DCPP), but our measurements show that this trades scheduling overhead for load balancing, which becomes unfavorable on long sequences. In this study, we propose Virtual Pipeline Parallelism (VPP), which keeps chunk sizes fixed and optimizes the pipeline layout through virtual stages." and "VPP improves throughput by up to 13.1% over DCPP on long sequences and 6.7% on mixed workloads, while preserving performance on short sequences. On a 512K-token DeepSeek-V3.1 prefill workload, VPP reduces the pipeline bubble ratio from 6.4% to 0.1%, achieving a 98.0% reduction compared with DCPP." The negative half of the same paper is ABANDONED-2.

title: Windowed-MTP — attention-sink + sliding-window KV budget validated at 1M tokens on ONE GPU

fields.detail: Retrieved abstract (title "[2607.21535] Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context", submitted 23 Jul 2026): "At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost". The paper's own method statement is the closest match in this whole subsection to a single-GPU, 1M-token, sink-based KV answer: "We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only ( Windowed-MTP ), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction : the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed , never which are accepted . It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ∼ 99 % {\sim}99\% of KV entries from the draft's read path at 1M." Setup section: "Unless noted, we evaluate on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU (tensor-parallel degree 1) with bf16 KV in SGLang … Windowed-MTP uses W = 4032 W{=}4032 , n sink = 64 n_{\text{sink}}{=}64 ."

title: How should a single long MLA prefill that carries existing context be scheduled chunk-by-chunk?

fields.who is still asking: LucasWilkinson (vLLM contributor), RFC #50497 "[RFC]: Per-request scheduling for MLA chunked context (prefill)"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "MLA prefill with existing context gathers paged latent KV into a fixed workspace, up-projects it, attends, and merges the partial into the running output. The schedule is **batch-column shaped** — the workspace is divided evenly across all prefills, and every iteration processes the same context window of **every** prefill (`build_mla_chunked_context_metadata()`, `vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/[mla_attention.py](...))"
fields.what specifically is missing: the RFC was closed as **completed** (`stateReason: COMPLETED`, created 2026-07-31T00:49:21Z) but the unanswered core is the *scheduling policy* — whether the workspace should be divided per-request rather than per-batch-column, and what the fairness/TTFT contract is when one request has a 1M-token context and others have short ones. No landed flag or default encodes a per-request MLA chunked-context schedule.

title: What owns KV memory for a request whose context never ends (streaming video, 1M-token sessions)?

fields.who is still asking: vLLM contributor, RFC #51948 "[RFC]: Bounded-memory video sessions — KV retention for long-running streaming-input requests"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Sessions exist; memory management for sessions does not." and, quoting vLLM's own streaming-input blog post back at the project: "additional care must be taken to avoid holding sessions open as they will be blocking the corresponding memory from being used by other requests… Currently, vLLM will not preempt "idle" streaming input sessions - this behaviour will be improved in a future update." and "One long-lived request that never ends. Two resources then grow without bound: GPU memory, since everything the model has seen stays resident for the life of the request (video is token-hungry - an hour at 2 fps is on the order of a million tokens of context); and sequence length, since the stream crosses the model's trained horizon within minutes to hours and output quality degrades past it."
fields.what specifically is missing: a KV retention/eviction policy for live sessions with unbounded context, and preemption of idle sessions. Streaming input exists (the cost-per-chunk problem is solved); bounded memory for it does not. State at retrieval: OPEN.

title: Per-token-range KV retention priority (protecting a shared system prompt's blocks from eviction) is proposed but not landed

fields.who is still asking: SGLang contributor, RFC #36208 "[RFC] Per-Token-Range KV-Cache Retention Priority"
fields.verbatim quote of the asking: "Today an SGLang request carries a single scalar `priority` applied uniformly to every RadixCache node it touches. This RFC proposes **per-token-range** retention priority: a request can say "give tokens `[0, 4)` priority 100, leave the rest at default," so KV-cache blocks covering a high-value prefix (e.g. a shared system prompt) are evicted later than lower-priority blocks, independently of the tokens that follow." and "Cross-session unfairness. Nothing stops the engine from evicting Session A's important prefix to make room for Session B's less-important request, even when A matters more — because "importance" is not expressible at sub-request granularity."
fields.what specifically is missing: the feature itself, plus a listed set of unresolved design pieces. The RFC's own Non-Goals section says priority decay "Deferred — not because it is unwanted, but because it can't be added cleanly on top of the current tree without its own design pass", and specifically that decay "interacts with chunked prefill and node splitting. Chunked prefill re-enters `_insert_helper` per chunk, and `_split_node` raises a question with no default answer (does a split-created node inherit the parent's remaining duration, or start a fresh clock?)." State at retrieval: OPEN, created 2026-08-24T17:09:43Z.

title: Dynamic chunk resizing for chunked-prefill pipeline parallelism (DCPP) — measured to LOSE on long sequences

fields.who: Yan Shi, Xiaochao Wang et al. (Huawei Technologies / Shanghai Jiao Tong University), the VPP paper's own negative result
fields.closure status: paper concludes the technique does NOT pay off at long context (negative result inside a published paper — the paper's own contribution is the opposite design, VPP).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Existing approaches mitigate this imbalance through dynamic chunk resizing (Dynamic CPP, DCPP), but our measurements show that this trades scheduling overhead for load balancing, which becomes unfavorable on long sequences." and, with the numbers: "At 512K, where the optimal chunk-size budget is 24K, profiler traces show that CPP requires 22 invocations, whereas DCPP requires 97, or 4.4 × 4.4\times as many." and "However, these savings are outweighed by the cost of finer-grained execution. Computation time increases by 10.5% (+26.48 s) as smaller chunks reduce operator efficiency, while the increased number of chunk boundaries raises exposed communication by 36.1% (+6.01 s). Despite dynamic balancing, 20.47 s of bubble remains, and DCPP ultimately incurs a 14.32 s (4.6%) TTFT regression over CPP." and "DCPP outperforms CPP on 64K–256K sequences, delivering consistent 1.6–3.6% improvements in both throughput and TTFT. However, its advantage progressively diminishes with sequence length and reverses at 512K, resulting in a 4.4% throughput loss and a 4.6% TTFT increase." and the generalisation: "These observations yield a critical insight: DCPP trades scheduling overhead for load-balancing gains. As sequence length grows, however, DCPP requires progressively more invocations, and the resulting fragmentation overhead eventually outweighs the benefits of bubble reduction."
fields.note: this is the *negative* half of the same paper whose positive half (VPP) is CLOSED-9.

title: Monolithic single-cartridge KV for a whole document collection — collapses to near-chance when composed

fields.who: Eyuboglu et al. (2025), the original Cartridges design — falsified by the CAS paper (arXiv:2606.04557), and by CAS's own limitations section
fields.closure status: published paper concludes the earlier technique does NOT pay off at collection scale (and the same paper's own limitations undercut parts of its own replacement).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "A critical limitation of this approach is that cartridges are monolithic and non-compositional: encoding an entire collection into a single KV block does not scale, and naively mixing cartridges trained in isolation collapses performance to near chance." and "However, their approach relies on a single monolithic cartridge per collection, which does not scale to real-world document collections: loading all documents into one cache bloats the prefix with irrelevant tokens, while information-dense content (e.g., financial tables, clinical notes, technical specifications) cannot be highly compressed without loss." - Inverted-negative from the CAS paper's OWN limitations section (its technique does not cover mid-conversation cache insertion at all): "In multi-turn scenarios, however, a cartridge may need to be loaded mid-conversation—for example, when a user references a new document after several turns of dialogue. Prepending the cartridge at that point would invalidate the previously computed KV entries, requiring a full recomputation of the conversation history." And the compression-tolerance bound: "Compression tolerance varies with document complexity ( 100 × 100\times for TechQA, ≤ 2 × {\leq}2\times for FinQA), reaching within 5% of uncompressed baselines. Finally, we show that cartridges can be combined with retrieval, matching RAG performance while using 3–4 × \times fewer tokens, though for information-dense tasks such as FinQA, text RAG maintains an edge." And on retrieval quality: "This is a pragmatic choice, but it means retrieval quality is bounded by how well the query matches the raw document text rather than the compressed KV representation."

title: "Dropping a KV row and seeing no accuracy loss" as validation of an eviction policy — shown to be an unsound inference

fields.who: Zefeng Cai, Zerui Cai (Independent Researchers) — "Compute Globally, Materialize Locally: The Memory Contract of Sparse Event-KV"
fields.closure status: published negative result that undercuts the standard validation methodology of long-context KV eviction/serving schemes (H2O-style, episodic-memory and agent-memory designs).
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "Long-horizon agents increasingly reuse their KV cache as memory: a serving system keeps a subset of cached entries and drops the rest. Eviction and episodic-memory schemes therefore rest on a premise rarely tested directly, that a retained event is still informative once the observations that produced it are gone." and the conclusion, verbatim: "One consequence follows for anyone who evicts. An ablation that drops a source event and observes no accuracy loss has not shown that the source was unnecessary; it may have retained a row that already carried the answer." and "For anyone who evicts the corollary is that dropping a source event and observing no accuracy loss does not show the source was unnecessary." - Second, separate negative inside the same paper (position-extension makes the null WORSE, not better): "16 16 of 20 20 conversations exceed Qwen3's native window, where restoring range with YaRN widens the null rather than closing it (both arms re-run together on one stack: LoCoMo − .048 -.048 [ − .103 , + .009 ] [-.103,+.009] without scaling, − .121 -.121 [ − .181 , − .068 ] [-.181,-.068] with it; paired per-conversation change − .074 -.074 , p = .02 p{=}.02 )."

title: Final-answer accuracy as the metric for KV compression at long context — shown to be an asymmetric (unsound) diagnostic

fields.who: Mengting Ai, Jingrui He, Yue Guo (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) — "Does Accuracy Equal Evidence? Reasoning Faithfulness under KV Cache Compression"
fields.closure status: published negative result whose own framing undercuts accuracy-only evaluation of long-context KV compression — including token-eviction families (recency/attention-sink, H2O/SnapKV-class) that this subsection covers.
fields.stated reason, verbatim: "KV cache compression is commonly evaluated by final-answer accuracy, implicitly assuming that preserving the answer also preserves the reasoning that supports it. We test this assumption for large reasoning models and show that it can fail: under compression, correct answers and the validity of their visible supporting rationales can be preserved at different rates." and "Across tasks, token-eviction methods can preserve competitive final-answer accuracy while substantially degrading chain support or perturbation faithfulness. We call this the answer-evidence gap." and "A coverage-preserving quantization control is substantially less affected, suggesting that the failure is tied less to KV memory reduction itself than to losing access to parts of the reasoning trace." and "we show that the final–answer accuracy is an asymmetric diagnostic for compressed reasoning. While collapsed accuracy reveals compression damage, preserved accuracy can hide evidence loss, creating an illusion of competence where correct answer lacks supported evidence." - Task-dependence, verbatim (which is what makes it usable as a scoping result): "Our results show that the answer–evidence gap is strongly task-dependent: on AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and MedCalc, compressed models can maintain competitive accuracy while reasoning validity or faithfulness substantially degrades. In contrast, on retrieval tasks such as RULER QA, where answers depend more directly on retaining exact supporting evidence, compression damage is more visible through accuracy collapse."

title: Decode context parallelism in SGLang (`--dcp-size`) — requires an existing tensor-parallel group

fields.hardware requirement: a TP group larger than the DCP size; the DCP group must nest inside one attention-TP group and one attention-DP replica (`attn_tp_size % dcp_size == 0`); communication backend resolves to `fi_a2a` only when the DCP group shares an MNNVL domain on Blackwell.
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Decode context parallelism (DCP) stripes a request’s MLA KV cache across ranks in an existing tensor-parallel group. With DCP size c , rank r owns position p when p mod c = r , so each rank stores and reads roughly 1/c of the cache." and "A DCP group must fit inside one attention-TP group and one attention-DP replica: Topology attn_tp_size = tp_size / attn_dp_size attn_tp_size % dcp_size == 0 For example, TP=64, DP=4, DCP=16 creates four valid 16-rank attention replicas. DCP=32 would cross replica boundaries and is invalid." and, for the Blackwell path specifically: "Unset resolves to fi_a2a where the DCP group shares an MNNVL domain on Blackwell, otherwise a2a on CUDA/ROCm." The documented enablement examples are all multi-GPU: "MLA decode on DeepSeek-V3.1 with DCP 8 inside TP 8" (`--tp-size 8 --dcp-size 8`), and "Kimi K3 on 32 GPUs with DPA and DCP 8".

title: Ring attention / partial-query–partial-KV prefill CP in vLLM — the only fully-general long-context KV path is explicitly still under development

fields.hardware requirement: multiple GPUs (`N` chunks for `N` GPUs); the full-KV variant additionally needs enough aggregate memory across ranks to hold gathered K/V.
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "During prefill, for a long request with `T` new tokens, we need to compute query/key/value tensors for these new tokens. Say we have `N` GPUs, we can split the request into `N` chunks, and each GPU computes one chunk of the query/key/value tensors." and "2. Partial query, partial key/value: If the request token length is too long, we cannot afford holding the full key/value tensors anymore, then we can only compute one chunk of query/key/value tensors for each GPU, and use techniques like [ring-attention](http://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01889) to send/recv key/value tensors chunk by chunk." and the status line: "Both approaches are under active development."

title: vLLM RFC — independent Context Parallelism for the DSA indexer

fields.hardware requirement: ≥2 GPUs in the CP group; the RFC's design evidence is measured on 2× NVIDIA H20.
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "Our preliminary operator benchmarks on 2x NVIDIA H20 report CP2 latency speedup as T(DCP=1) / T(DCP=2) . Each panel fixes batch size and query length; the x-axis is history length. The Indexer obtains substantially higher CP2 speedup than Sparse MLA across most long-context Q>1 shapes, while both stages regress at Q=1 because communication and launch overheads dominate." The RFC further states the coupling that makes it a CP-only feature: "vLLM currently derives both stages' parallel rank, group, and world size from the same Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) configuration."

title: Cartridges at Scale (CAS) — training modular KV caches over large document collections

fields.hardware requirement: a multi-GPU cluster (NVIDIA H200 and B200 cloud GPUs), plus persistent storage for cartridge rotation; the training pool holds a bounded number of cartridges on GPU with the rest offloaded.
fields.verbatim evidence of the requirement: "We train using a cluster with NVidia H200 and B200 cloud GPUs." and "In this work, we introduce CAS, a framework for training and deploying cartridges at scale over collections of hundreds of documents and millions of tokens. CAS proposes a training regime based on dynamic cartridge rotation and mixing that closes the performance gap of isolated training (Fig.  1 ) while remaining feasible within current GPU memory constraints." and "We propose CAS, a scalable training framework with GPU ↔ \leftrightarrow persistent storage swapping, optimizer offloading, and prioritized rotation, enabling joint training of hundreds of cartridges within a fixed GPU memory budget." Also: "with all 20 cartridges active simultaneously (no rotation needed for 20 cartridges on a H100 GPU)".

title: Continuum / CacheTTL — KV cache time-to-live

fields.detail: A published serving system whose core mechanism is a per-request KV TTL derived from reload cost plus queueing-delay cost. Abs page (v7) title verbatim: "Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live". Abstract verbatim: "We present Continnum, a serving system to optimize job completion time for multi-turn agent workloads by introducing time-to-live mechanism for KV cache retention. For requests that generate tool calls, Continnum selectively pins the KV cache in GPU memory with a time-to-live value determined by the reload cost and potential queueing delay induced by eviction. When the TTL expires, the KV cache can be automatically evicted to free up GPU memory, providing robust performance under edge cases." Also verbatim: "Evaluations on real-world agents (SWE-Bench, BFCL, OpenHand) with Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Gemma-3 12B, and GLM-4.5 355B shows that Continnum improves the average job completion times by over 8x while improving throughput." Version note: at v4 the same arXiv ID was titled "CacheTTL: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live"; the v7 abstract misspells the system as "Continnum".

title: vLLM NIXL KV lease renewal TTL

fields.detail: Merged 2026-05-11 ("NickLucche merged commit 770e9bd into vllm-project : main"). Replaces a single fixed abort timeout with a renewable lease. PR body verbatim: "TL;DR: VLLM_NIXL_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT single timeout is too simple and leads to P holding requests for too long when D crashes. We need a more dynamic TTL “lease renewal” system that minimizes the time blocks are stranded on P. At the same time, we also need a way for D to extend TTL of requests blocks in P that are currently in the waiting queue. This ensures traffic surges on D do not lead to blocks “early-free” due to congestion". Shipped knobs shown verbatim in the test plan: "initial_kv_lease": 20, "heartbeat_interval": 3, "heartbeat_lease_extension": 10.

title: ARC eviction policy for the CPU KV-offload tier

fields.detail: Merged 2025-11-12 by maintainer ApostaC ("ApostaC merged commit bac9045 into vllm-project : main Nov 12, 2025"). Body verbatim: "Current vLLM v1 uses LRU for KV cache eviction, which works well for scan-heavy workloads but can struggle with mixed access patterns. ARC automatically adapts between recency-based (LRU-like) and frequency-based (LFU-like) eviction, providing better cache efficiency for diverse workloads." Scope caveat established by this PR's own test path: its test suite is "tests/kv_offload/test_cpu_manager.py", i.e. this is the *CPU offload* replacement policy, not the GPU block pool's. Follow-on merged work referenced on the page: vllm-project/vllm#50992 "[Perf][KV Offload] Avoid quadratic ARC batch eviction" (Merged).

title: KV block residency / lifetime metrics

fields.detail: vLLM ships sampled per-block lifetime instrumentation. Verbatim from the design doc: "We also emit a set of histograms that describe how long sampled KV cache blocks stay resident and how often they are reused. Sampling (`--kv-cache-metrics-sample`) keeps the overhead tiny; when a block is chosen we record:" followed by "- `lifetime` – allocation ⟶ eviction", "- `idle before eviction` – last touch ⟶ eviction", "- `reuse gaps` – the pauses between touches when the block gets reused", and "Those map directly to the Prometheus metrics:" / "- `vllm:kv_block_lifetime_seconds` – how long each sampled block exists." / "- `vllm:kv_block_idle_before_evict_seconds` – idle tail after the final access." / "- `vllm:kv_block_reuse_gap_seconds` – time between consecutive touches." Implementation confirmed by reading the source file (raw): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_metrics.py defines `class KVCacheMetricsCollector`, `get_lifetime_seconds`, `get_idle_time_seconds`, `get_reuse_gaps_seconds`, `on_block_allocated`, `on_block_accessed`, `on_block_evicted`. Doct text also states verbatim: "The engine core only ships raw eviction events via `SchedulerStats`; the frontend drains them, turns them into Prometheus observations".

title: vLLM V1 preemption mode is RECOMPUTE, not SWAP

fields.detail: Merged. PR body verbatim: "In the V1 engine, num_cpu_blocks is hardcoded to 0 ( v1/engine/core.py:287 ), confirming swap space was never allocated or used." Shipped decision documented verbatim at https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/configuration/optimization.md: "In vLLM V1, the default preemption mode is `RECOMPUTE` rather than `SWAP`, as recomputation has lower overhead in the V1 architecture." Rationale for the historical choice, verbatim from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/metrics.md: "Later, the concept of prefix caching was introduced, which allowed KV cache blocks to be shared implicitly. This proved to be a better option than CPU swapping since blocks can be evicted slowly on demand and the part of the prompt that was evicted can be recomputed."

title: SGLang HiCache — KV as a GPU/CPU/storage hierarchy

fields.detail: Shipped, documented feature. Retrieved page title verbatim: "Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache) - SGLang Documentation"; the page links sub-pages at /docs/advanced_features/hicache_best_practices, /docs/advanced_features/hicache_design and /docs/advanced_features/hicache_storage_runtime_attach_detach, and offers an "llms.txt" documentation index. Operator-facing behavior is stated verbatim in the SGLang cookbook source retrieved from GitHub raw (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sgl-project/sglang/main/docs/cookbook/autoregressive/DeepSeek/DeepSeek-V4_1.mdx): "the Playground emits `--enable-hierarchical-cache` on top of the recipe's flags, and cold KV pages spill to CPU pinned memory (L2, GPU + CPU) instead of being dropped from the GPU pool. The host pool is sized by ratio (`--hicache-ratio 2`), not by a fixed `--hicache-size`." Write policies, verbatim from the same file: "The Write policy knob controls the GPU → CPU write and defaults to `write_through` (the upstream default): every page is mirrored to the CPU tier as it is written. `write_through_selective` backs up only hot data and `write_back` defers the copy to eviction, trading cache freshness for host-side I/O." Tier scope, verbatim: "Only the L2 tier is exposed here. For the storage (L3) tier and the canonical flag set, see the [HiCache best-practices recipe]".

title: SGLang `--radix-eviction-policy` (lru / lfu / slru / priority)

fields.detail: Shipped, documented eviction policies with a policy-config surface. Verbatim from the page: "Select one with --radix-eviction-policy . All of them fall back to least-recently-used order within a tie." The policy table is verbatim: "lru (default) The prefix unused for longest. General serving. Matches how prefix reuse decays with time." / "lfu The prefix with the fewest cache hits, then the least recent. A small set of prompts is reused far more than the rest, and you want those to survive bursts of one-off traffic." / "slru Prefixes still in the probationary segment, then the least recent within a segment." / "priority The prefix belonging to the lowest-priority request, then the least recent. You run priority scheduling and want cache retention to follow the same ranking as admission." Scoring caveats, verbatim: "Hit count ( lfu , slru ) counts how many times a node was matched by a later request. It is not incremented for chunked-prefill steps, for evicted nodes, or under write-back HiCache." and "Without priority scheduling every node is priority 0 and this policy is equivalent to lru ." Guidance, verbatim: "Start with lru and change it only against a measured cache hit rate — the counters are exposed under --enable-metrics ." Tuning is via `--radix-eviction-policy-config` (e.g. `{"protected_threshold": 4}`).

title: SGLang Session-Aware Radix Cache

fields.detail: Shipped application-lifetime KV retention. Verbatim: "Session-aware radix caching improves cache hits for long-lived, multi-turn workloads under memory pressure. It registers reusable KV to a session and evicts unreferenced KV before KV still referenced by an active session." Explicitly soft, verbatim: "Session references are soft protection, not memory pins. Referenced KV can still be evicted when reclaiming unreferenced KV is insufficient." Enablement verbatim: "SGLANG_ENABLE_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE = 1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path MODEL_PATH --enable-session-radix-cache", with lifecycle via `curl -X POST http://localhost:30000/close_session -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"session_id": "agent-42"}'`. Eviction order verbatim: "Unreferenced nodes first, then referenced nodes with fewer session references, then the configured policy such as LRU". Restriction verbatim: "This feature is implemented only by UnifiedRadixCache ."

title: vToken — token-level virtualization for reclaimable KV

fields.detail: Abstract verbatim: "We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously." Result verbatim: "Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50." Setup, verbatim from https://arxiv.org/html/2608.13263v1 §5.1: "We evaluate vToken on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU with 80 GB of memory." and §4: "The prototype targets the single-node, single-GPU decoding fast path, isolating the interaction between token-level eviction and block-managed KV allocation without conflating it with distributed scheduling or cross-device KV movement." Implemented in "vLLM (v0.18.0), using PyTorch v2.10.0". Self-scoped limits, verbatim from §6 Discussion: "Our current implementation uses one runtime KV cache group and conservatively skips shared-prefix blocks to preserve prefix-cache correctness."

title: PrefixShield — admission responsibility in multi-tenant prefix caches

fields.detail: Abstract verbatim: "A group that materializes new Key-Value (KV) blocks can force another to lose reusable state, yet request-time schedulers account for transient service, replacement policies primarily rank object value, and static partitioning strands idle capacity. We call this mismatch the admission-responsibility gap." Mechanism and result verbatim: "we propose PrefixShield, which meters newly materialized full KV blocks, carries responsibility across requests, gates reuse promotion while debt remains, and uses projected debt to select the group supplying eviction candidates. We implement PrefixShield in vLLM." Numbers verbatim: "In paired runs under one-touch pollution, PrefixShield improves victim cache hit ratio by 9.39 percentage points over the Least Recently Used (LRU) policy and 8.64 points over S3-FIFO, restoring the victim from 4.92% to 84.87% at 4096-block scale, and gains 2.00 points over S3-FIFO under two-pass replay." Conclusion verbatim: "These results show that object-value signals rank what to retain, while persistent responsibility determines which group bears reclamation pressure."

title: Leyline — KV cache directives for in-place span editing

fields.detail: Abstract verbatim: "Agentic LLMs break this assumption. Their conversations evolve through policy-driven editing: failed tool calls are retried, stale outputs dropped, trajectories pivoted." and "a policy may need to direct the serving system to actively remove or replace a span of cached content and continue without re-prefilling everything that came after. No existing primitive offers this. Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost; kernel-level eviction methods make their own decisions and cannot accept policy directives from outside the kernel." Result verbatim: "The splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241 ms. A ten-line truncation rule routed through the same interface lifts agentic solve rate by +14.3 pp on debug-gym. The mechanism is open; the policy space it enables is the agenda."
